  "article": "## The model being tested\n\nOn each of [LP2-33](#/reader/lp2-33) and [LP2-39](#/reader/lp2-39), label the three horizontal dots A, B and C from left to right. Draw three circles centered at those dots. Can the circles meet at one point on each page if **the same ordered radii** are used on both pages?\n\nThe two target points may differ. The radius at A must be the same on both pages, likewise B and C. Both pages remain at their original 2400 × 3600 pixel scale; no resizing or refitting is allowed. This is one precise compass construction, not a general test of compass-related ideas.\n\n**Result: no**, for the measured dot centers at each of the three declared grayscale thresholds. An exact rational distance bound rules out every possible ordered radius triple within this model. It does not require selecting radii from the number square or searching a finite list.\n\n## Measure the centers first\n\nThe script reads the original JPEGs, converts RGB to Pillow’s L grayscale, and finds four-connected dark components inside two declared crop boxes. Pixel coordinates are zero-based, with integer coordinates at pixel centers. Crop right and bottom edges are exclusive.\n\n| Page | Crop (left, top, right, bottom) |\n| --- | --- |\n| LP2-33 | (576, 1656, 1824, 1836) |\n| LP2-39 | (1200, 1638, 1800, 1746) |\n\nFor each threshold 100, 140 and 180, a pixel is dark if its grayscale value is strictly below the threshold. Retain components with area greater than 200 pixels, width/height strictly between 0.7 and 1.3, and filled area greater than 60% of the bounding rectangle. Exactly three components must survive; otherwise the script stops.\n\nEach center is the arithmetic mean of its component’s pixel coordinates. The report stores integer coordinate sums and areas, so the subsequent calculation uses exact fractions rather than rounded coordinates. This measures a particular thresholded shape; it is not an assertion that the author placed the dot at that exact rational point.\n\nThe source-region figure shows decoded original JPEG crops with red center marks. It does not threshold or increase contrast in the displayed image; thresholding is used only to calculate the marked centers. Each crop is fitted to the same display width, so the previews have different scales. The separate spacing diagram uses a common horizontal scale.\n\nAt threshold 140, the adjacent center separations on LP2-33 are approximately 417.47 and 478.23 pixels. On LP2-39 they are 196 and 224.5 pixels. The diagram uses one horizontal scale for both pages and separates the rows vertically for readability. It does not show the original vertical positions.\n\n## Why three distances impose a constraint\n\nLet Q be the perpendicular projection of B onto the line through A and C. Write `Q=(1−t)A+tC` and `e=B−Q`. The dots are almost collinear; e measures the middle dot’s small displacement from that line. Let `K=t(1−t)|C−A|²`.\n\nIf X is a target point with distances rA, rB and rC from the three dots, expanding the squared distances gives:\n\n```text\nrB² − (1−t)rA² − t rC² + K\n  = 2 e·(Q−X) + |e|²\n```\n\nThe right-hand side is an affine function of X. Its minimum and maximum over a rectangle occur at corners, so evaluating the four page corners gives an exact residual interval. No grid sampling of target points is necessary.\n\nNow compare the two pages. Their shared radii cancel except for `(t₂−t₁)(rA²−rC²)`. Each squared radius lies between zero and the squared page diagonal, because both its center and target lie on the page. Consequently:\n\n```text\n|residual₂ − residual₁|\n  ≥ |K₂ − K₁| − |t₂ − t₁| × (2399² + 3599²)\n```\n\nThe two corner intervals also give an upper bound on that absolute difference. If the lower bound exceeds the upper bound, no target pair with shared radii can exist.\n\n## The bounds\n\nThe table rounds displayed values to two decimal places. Decisions use exact fractions saved in the report; the unit is squared pixels.\n\n| Threshold | Required lower bound | Allowed upper bound | Compatible? |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| 100 | 153,322.33 | 119.47 | No |\n| 140 | 155,146.71 | 14.17 | No |\n| 180 | 153,854.17 | 11.88 | No |\n\nAll three declared threshold variants give the same exclusion. This is a sensitivity check, not a confidence interval or a complete treatment of measurement error. The argument treats each measured center as fixed; it does not quantify every plausible alternative center, crop or dot-selection rule.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the experiment bundle, then extract the [original-images ZIP](downloads/original-images.zip) into the same folder so that `images/lp2-33.jpg` and `images/lp2-39.jpg` are available. Original images are separate from the small experiment ZIP. Install Pillow 11.3.0 in your Python environment, then verify the required image hashes and run:\n\n```text\npython scripts/verify_bundle.py EXPERIMENT-compass-shared-radii-IMAGE-INPUTS.json\npython experiments/records/compass-shared-radii/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/compass-shared-radii/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer uses Pillow 11.3.0 and Python’s standard library. Its version is recorded so a different image-decoding environment does not silently claim an exact replay. The checker needs only the standard library. Neither command calls AI or accesses the network.\n\nThe producer reruns component measurement, the rational certificate and the annotated source-region SVG. The separate checker verifies source hashes and reconstructs the projection parameter from squared side lengths. It obtains residuals by directly expanding distances to the page corners, without importing the producer. It verifies that identical page geometry is not rejected by the bound. It does **not** independently segment the images or provide a manual review of the dots.\n\nBoth checks passed on 20 October 2026. The procedure and controls were recorded in `plan.txt`; the declared thresholds, crops and target rectangle were unchanged after the run. This freshly reconstructs a constrained claim in the supplied research archive; it is not a new discovery. Human review remains pending.\n\n## What remains outside this result\n\nRescaling one page, using different radii on each page, changing which dots receive which radii, placing a target outside the page, stepping a compass between points, or reading pairwise intersections changes the model. Those alternatives are not excluded here. The result supplies no rune selection or plaintext claim.\n\nFor the distinction between an illustration and a specified cipher, see [compass constructions](#/wiki/compass-cipher-tests). For coordinate conventions and original files, see [image regions](#/wiki/image-regions). For how to state this exclusion without overstating it, see [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space).\n",

  "article": "## The question this comparison asks\n\nAn earlier word-length analysis compared the unsolved manuscript with thousands of converted texts. Before interpreting a reported rarity, we need to know what was counted, which texts entered the comparison, and whether repeated files received repeated weight.\n\nThis experiment asks a specific descriptive question: **where does the reconstructed 2,902-token manuscript summary fall among the first 2,902 tokens of every eligible file in the pinned reference corpus?** It does not ask which language is most likely. The separate [parallel-language experiments](#/experiments/parallel-languages) compare aligned translations under declared representations.\n\n## What the complete audit found\n\nThe census covers all **25,906 paths** and **25,844 distinct source blobs**. Of these, **25,565 paths** are long enough for the declared prefix, representing **25,563 distinct eligible blobs**. The other 341 paths are retained as ineligible rows. Every source object and all 46 comparison rows passed the separate checks.\n\nThe manuscript has 448 length-two tokens out of 2,902. Only 138 eligible prefixes have a smaller proportion, and one ties it: the inclusive fraction at or below is **139/25,565 (about 0.544%)**. Its 720 length-three tokens give a different position: 24,171 prefixes fall below that proportion, 29 tie it and 1,365 fall above it. These are descriptive counts within this reference collection, not chances that a language or cipher hypothesis is true.\n\nOther measures need not be extreme. The manuscript's variance has 10,995 prefixes below it and 14,570 above it. Its minimum token length of one ties every eligible prefix. Its lack of tokens of length 15 or more is shared by 13,205 prefixes. The complete tables retain these ordinary and tied observations alongside the more unusual proportions.\n\nRemoving byte-identical duplication reduces the eligible denominator by only two. For the length-two proportion, the below and equal counts remain 138 and one; the above count changes from 25,426 to 25,424. This sensitivity removes duplicate bytes, not all related works.\n\n## Why 2,902 rather than 2,896?\n\nThe [word-length guide](#/wiki/word-lengths?section=historical-count) reconstructs the historical summary by including six isolated digits alongside 2,896 rune tokens. Counting each digit as a length-one token reproduces the earlier summary. This does not make those digits runes, nor prove what the original author's parser intended.\n\nThe target for this experiment is that reconstructed historical summary. Switching to the rune-only target would change both the denominator and the reference-prefix length. It belongs in an explicitly declared variant, not an unnoticed correction during the calculation.\n\n## What enters the reference population?\n\nThe pinned source tree contains 25,906 paths under `files/`. Every path is considered. A file is eligible when it has at least 2,902 nonempty tokens separated by the literal space character. Its first 2,902 tokens form its profile; later material is not sampled.\n\nThere is no language selection, header removal or filtering to the 29-rune alphabet. Strict UTF-8 decoding is required. Token length is the number of retained Unicode code points. A newline or another non-space character remains part of its token under this rule. This precision matters: a general whitespace splitter would implement a different experiment.\n\nThe [earlier twelve-prefix audit](#/wiki/word-lengths?section=corpus-inputs) found symbols outside the stored manuscript alphabet. The full census preserves the declared counting rule rather than silently deleting them. Relabeling a symbol one-for-one preserves length; deleting it can change lengths, empty tokens and subsequent prefix selection.\n\n## Two ways to weight the same files\n\nThe primary comparison counts every eligible path. If two filenames contain identical bytes, both contribute. This preserves the historical file-based population.\n\nThe sensitivity comparison counts each distinct eligible Git blob once. This removes byte-identical duplication. It does not deduplicate editions, translations, differently formatted copies or separate excerpts from the same work. Consequently, neither population should be described as thousands of independent books.\n\nBoth versions show the same 23 measures: proportions of lengths 1 through 14 and 15+, mean, sample variance, sample standard deviation, minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum. The 15+ bin retains longer reference tokens even though the manuscript target has none. Measures are related; they are not 23 independent experiments.\n\n## How to read the figure and exact tables\n\nEach bar divides the reference population into values strictly below, equal to and strictly above the manuscript value. “Below” is a numerical relation, not a judgement of which text is more natural or more similar overall. For example, a prefix below the manuscript's length-two proportion simply contains a smaller proportion of length-two tokens.\n\nThe tables also retain two inclusive fractions: `(below + equal) / total` and `(above + equal) / total`. Ties enter both. With three reference values below the target, two equal and five above, the fractions are 5/10 and 7/10. They sum to more than one because both include the two ties. Subtracting either fraction from one would give the other *strict* side, not the other inclusive fraction.\n\nCounts, means, variances and interpolated quartiles are compared using exact rational arithmetic. Standard deviation is ranked through variance, because taking a nonnegative square root preserves order and ties. Rounded values displayed to readers do not decide equality.\n\n## What an extreme rank would establish\n\nAn extreme rank means that few of these particular file prefixes fall on one side of the manuscript under the specified counting rule. It is not a probability that the plaintext is English, a probability that the manuscript is natural language, or a calibrated hypothesis-test p-value.\n\nThe collection is fixed and nonrandom; its edition manifest and conversion procedure remain unavailable. File beginnings can contain material unlike the manuscript. Corpus units count all retained Unicode code points, while the target counts runes plus six digits. These limitations remain even if the arithmetic is reproduced exactly.\n\nFor a one-symbol-for-one-symbol cipher with preserved boundaries, plaintext and ciphertext token lengths agree. A mismatch with a reference corpus still does not identify a length-changing cipher: the text's genre, conversion rules, headings and boundary conventions can also differ. See [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) and [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space).\n\n## Reproduce the comparison\n\nFrom a Liberpedia checkout or complete reproduction bundle, with an existing local corpus clone and a new output directory:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/corpus-prefix-census/run.py /path/to/project-runeberg --output /path/to/new-corpus-replay\n```\n\nPython's standard library and Git are sufficient. The wrapper runs offline and stops when any stage fails. The [reproduction instructions](experiments/records/corpus-prefix-census/README.md) explain source retrieval, each output, and how to resume an interrupted census. The external corpus is not included in the reproduction bundle.\n\nThe source checker reads every distinct blob, independently reconstructs the token prefix and statistics, and checks every duplicate row. A second checker independently reconstructs all 46 comparison rows with exact ties. Only after both succeed does the renderer create the figure and tables. These are separate implementations within this project, not an external peer review.\n\n## Sources and scope\n\nThe corpus is [mortlach/project-runeberg at revision a39e87e](https://github.com/mortlach/project-runeberg/tree/a39e87ece3e6cbb0f00f7ad5fff9183da5c66d87). The earlier analysis is [mae3301/lp_experiments at revision cb5cdb9](https://github.com/mae3301/lp_experiments/tree/cb5cdb908bb34b68d8a05353eaace56e83d0bbf2). The census and comparison plans retain the counting conventions and input hashes fixed before the complete run.\n\nThe [provenance note](experiments/records/corpus-prefix-census/PROVENANCE.md) preserves a frozen test-file hash and documents corruption checks added later. The calculation and audit code match their recorded hashes.\n\nThis is a fresh implementation of a declared descriptive comparison. It does not execute the historical scripts, validate their entire statistical analysis, or reproduce an unavailable conversion pipeline.\n\n## Complete corpus comparison\n\nEvery planned measure is shown under both weighting rules. Bars partition reference prefixes by whether their value is below, equal to, or above the manuscript value. They do not show probabilities of a language or cipher.\n\nThe two inclusive fractions both contain ties: they can sum to more than one. Distinct Git blobs remove byte-identical duplicates only; editions, translations and overlapping works may remain. Manuscript values are exact fractions; length-bin values are proportions. Standard deviation is shown as a square root, while its ranks use exact variance ordering, which preserves all ties.\n\n### Every eligible path\n\n| Measure | Manuscript value | Below | Equal | Above   "article": "## The comparison\n\nThe pale tree on [LP2-55](#/reader/lp2-55) resembles the photograph [DeadTree.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DeadTree.jpg), credited to R. Neil Marshman / Brookie. This test asks a narrower, checkable question: when the source photograph is scaled and translated over the manuscript tree, does a horizontal reflection fit better than its original orientation? It does **not** seek a decryption rule or recover the original image-editing steps.\n\nThe published [Commons original](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg) is 1,894 × 2,606 pixels. Its local SHA-256 is `608288991f92b8ab901a9fbb39937f93ebdfeb5fd84edeecfa637d5262ff7b29`; its SHA-1 matches the checksum on the [Commons file record](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DeadTree.jpg). The LP2-55 JPEG is the archived 2,400 × 3,600-pixel page. The script rejects either image if its bytes change.\n\n![Mirrored source, pale manuscript tree and their half-opacity overlay](exports/figures/dead-tree-alignment.png)\n\nThe figure shows the selected mirrored fit at left, the LP2-55 tree region in the middle and a 50% overlay at right. Both source and manuscript are converted to grayscale response maps, enlarged for inspection; this is **not** an unmodified image or a reconstruction of the author’s layer. The source is R. Neil Marshman / Brookie, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/), horizontally reflected, cropped, resized, threshold-mapped and blurred here. [Open the original photograph](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg) · [Open the unmodified manuscript page](images/lp2-55.jpg).\n\n## Frozen comparison rule\n\nThe source crop is `[100, 500, 1750, 1950]`; the LP2-55 crop is `[550, 1300, 1850, 2550]`, with right and bottom edges excluded. In each grayscale crop, values darker than the chosen brightness level become a stronger tree response. The source uses `clip((170−L)/130,0,1)` and the manuscript `clip((250−L)/45,0,1)`. Gaussian blur with sigma 7 tolerates differences in stroke width and some missing twigs. Those values were chosen after inspecting the images, so the following scores are descriptive rather than a blind significance test.\n\nFor each orientation, the script checks 23 scales from 0.370 through 0.700 in increments of 0.015, plus every integer translation that keeps the whole template inside the manuscript crop. The fit score is normalized cross-correlation. In a second run, only the upper 60% of the source template chooses the transform; the lower 40% is scored at that fixed transform. This lower-region check tests whether the upper-branch fit extends further down the same image. It is not a wholly independent holdout because the photograph, crops and processing were selected after viewing both images.\n\n| Orientation | Best whole-crop correlation | Upper 60% fit | Lower 40% at that fit |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Original | 0.377 | 0.564 | −0.095 |\n| Horizontal reflection | **0.623** | **0.813** | **0.456** |\n\nThe reflected upper fit uses scale 0.550 and translation `(230,94)` relative to the LP2-55 crop. Its major forks, central branch structure and rightward lower limb overlap in the visualization. The unreflected comparison does not carry its upper fit into the lower region. [Download every scale, coordinate and score](exports/dead-tree-alignment.json).\n\n## What this establishes and what remains open\n\nThe two declared alignments favor a horizontally reflected source photograph, including the lower region that did not choose the fit. This supports a specific image-source relationship more strongly than a general resemblance between bare trees. The test does not calculate a chance probability against a collection of other tree photographs. It does not establish the exact crop, layer opacity, drawing/filter steps or software used to make LP2-55. Fine branches and the lower trunk differ visibly in the overlay.\n\nThe [branches guide](#/wiki/branches?section=shared-tree) compares the related treatments on LP2-32 and in the 2016 message. Those carriers are **not** fit by this script. A <a href=\"#/experiments/dead-tree-cross-carrier\">related experiment</a> now gives each its own crop, response rule and orientation control. Nothing in this image alignment implies a rune operation.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nDownload the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/dead-tree-alignment.zip) and extract it preserving folders. It contains the [Commons original](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg). Download the [LP2-55 original](images/lp2-55.jpg) separately or extract the original-images ZIP into the same folder. Install Python 3, NumPy and OpenCV (`opencv-python`); the recorded run used OpenCV 5.0.0. Verify the files using the bundled `START-HERE` instructions, then run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/dead-tree-alignment/run.py --check\n```\n\nTo regenerate a report and figure under other settings, edit a **copy** of the script and save separate outputs. Report altered crops, thresholds, blur, scale range and orientation choices. The exact source file, [plan](experiments/records/dead-tree-alignment/plan.txt), [script](experiments/records/dead-tree-alignment/run.py), [results](exports/dead-tree-alignment.json) and [visualization](exports/figures/dead-tree-alignment.png) are linked here for inspection.\n",

  "article": "## One source family, two different treatments\n\nThe [LP2-55 source comparison](#/experiments/dead-tree-alignment) favored a horizontally reflected version of R. Neil Marshman’s [DeadTree.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DeadTree.jpg). Two related images remain: a broad, soft tree on [LP2-32](#/reader/lp2-32), and a faint tree behind text in the [2016 message](images/message-2016.jpg). This record measures them separately. The first comparison uses LP2-55 as the reference image; the second returns to the Commons photograph. It does not assume identical blur, brightness or scale across carriers.\n\nThe result supports the shared tree artwork under the declared comparisons. It does not recover how the author processed any image, prove a decryption step or assign a probability of chance resemblance across other photographs.\n\n## LP2-55 → LP2-32: same orientation\n\nThe script compares the tree region of two original 2,400 × 3,600 JPEGs. It maps their differently rendered dark and pale shapes to grayscale responses, blurs with sigma 15 and searches scales 0.650–1.225 in 0.025 steps. It searches every integer translation keeping the source crop fully inside the LP2-32 crop. Both the original LP2-55 orientation and its horizontal reflection are scored.\n\n![LP2-55 tree aligned to LP2-32, with target and overlay](exports/figures/dead-tree-manuscript.png)\n\nThe displayed panels are contrast-mapped and blurred for this comparison; open the [unmodified LP2-55](images/lp2-55.jpg) and [LP2-32](images/lp2-32.jpg) images to inspect the real artwork. The unchanged orientation aligns the broad top forks and carries more of that alignment into the lower trunk. The figure shows its upper-region fit and a half-opacity overlay, not an original image layer.\n\n| LP2-55 orientation | Whole-region best | Upper 60% fit | Lower 40% at upper fit |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Same | **0.623** | **0.704** | **0.600** |\n| Horizontally reflected | 0.483 | 0.514 | 0.353 |\n\nThe same-orientation upper fit uses scale 0.900 and translation `(123,186)` inside the LP2-32 crop. This says that the two *manuscript treatments* preserve orientation relative to each other. It does not contradict the preceding experiment, where both were compared with an originally unreflected photograph.\n\n## Commons photograph → 2016: reflected orientation\n\nThe 2016 JPEG is only 563 × 569 pixels and puts pale message text over a very dark tree. The script crops the central tree, maps pixel brightness above the black background to a response, and masks pixels brighter than 100 to reduce the white lettering. It uses Gaussian sigma 1.5 and searches 26 scales from 0.065 to 0.140. The source photograph’s original and horizontally reflected orientations are both compared.\n\n![Mirrored Commons tree aligned to the faint 2016 background tree, with target and overlay](exports/figures/dead-tree-message.png)\n\nThis figure increases contrast and removes much of the bright text **for inspection only**; it is not the original message. The source photograph is R. Neil Marshman / Brookie, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/), cropped, mirrored, resized and contrast-mapped here. [Original Commons JPEG](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg) · [original 2016 message](images/message-2016.jpg).\n\n| Photograph orientation | Whole-region best | Upper 60% fit | Lower 40% at upper fit |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Original | 0.566 | 0.644 | 0.442 |\n| Horizontal reflection | **0.854** | **0.826** | **0.858** |\n\nThe reflected upper fit uses scale 0.089 and translation `(69,29)` within the message crop. The lower region matches at that fixed transform despite not setting the transform in the declared search. The photograph, crop, text mask and response were still chosen after seeing the images, so these correlations are descriptive, **not** a calibrated chance probability.\n\n## Bounds, files and next checks\n\nThe [complete result JSON](exports/dead-tree-cross-carrier.json) records both orientations, 24 and 26 scale values, crops, settings, coordinates and scores. This is one family of related source-image comparisons, not a blanket assertion that every tree image was made with the same filter. Fine branches and the amount of visible trunk vary. No source was inferred from manuscript text or rune values.\n\nThe lower 40% check is useful but not fully independent: all preprocessing choices and the two target images were selected during exploration. A stronger source-identification test would score a preregistered set of unrelated tree photographs under the same search budget and report the winner and gap. An exact production reconstruction would need to explain the tonal treatment and branch omissions as well as geometry. Those questions remain open.\n\nDownload the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/dead-tree-cross-carrier.zip); it contains the Commons photograph, plan, script, report and figures. Place the original LP2-55, LP2-32 and 2016 JPEGs in its `images/` directory, or extract the site’s original-images ZIP there. Install Python 3, NumPy and OpenCV (the recorded run used OpenCV 5.0.0), verify the bundled files and image hashes using the `START-HERE` instructions, then run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/dead-tree-cross-carrier/run.py --check\n```\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/dead-tree-cross-carrier/plan.txt) lists every input and preprocessing choice. Edit a copy and save separate results for any changed crop, mask, threshold, scale range or image set. The [script](experiments/records/dead-tree-cross-carrier/run.py) does not access a network or AI service.\n",

  "article": "## Can a correct key still fail?\n\nYes, under a mismatched decoding rule. This experiment starts with known rune sequences, encrypts them using four precisely specified mechanisms, and asks what rigid subtraction and a skip-aware beam decoder recover. Knowing the answer lets us measure exact recovery rather than judging whether a candidate merely sounds plausible.\n\nAll ordinary-addition controls recover exactly with the correct key. With key skipping and single-value keys, the beam allowing three skips recovers 26 of 27 plants exactly, while rigid subtraction recovers one. Repeating each key value four times changes that result: the same beam recovers eight of 27, with the true recorded alignment outside its transition rules in the other 19. Increasing beam width from 16 to 64 does not repair that structural limit.\n\nThese findings concern the declared artificial encoders. They do not show that the unsolved manuscript uses key skipping, rewriting, or any particular key generator.\n\n## Four ways to consume the same key\n\nEvery operation uses rune indices modulo 29. Ordinary addition emits `c = p + k`; subtraction recovers `p = c − k`. A key slot is a position in the generated sequence, not its numerical value. Several slots can hold the same value.\n\n| Encoder | What happens when the proposed ciphertext repeats the previous rune? | Key alignment |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Ordinary addition | Emit it unchanged. | One slot per plaintext rune. |\n| Key skipping | With probability 83/100, reject that key slot and retry the same plaintext rune. | Rejections consume additional slots. |\n| Value rewriting | With probability 83/100, add one to the proposed ciphertext value modulo 29. | Still one slot per plaintext rune. |\n| Unrelated advance plus skipping | Apply the skip rule, but also consume one extra slot halfway through the plaintext, regardless of repetition. | Contains an advance that the collision-only model may not permit. |\n\nThe first emitted rune has no predecessor. The rejection draw occurs only on a collision. Each plant resets its state, and every draw, rejected slot, accepted slot and rewrite is preserved in the report. Exhausting the key is an error; no zero padding is allowed.\n\nThe key fixture hashes a fixed seed label and counter with SHA-256, then reduces each byte modulo 29. This reduction is biased because 256 is not divisible by 29. It is a reproducible test input, not a claim of uniform randomness or a one-time pad. The second fixture repeats each value across four successive slots. Neither fixture was adjusted to match manuscript statistics.\n\nFor an introductory numerical diagram, see [key alignment, skip limits and beam search](#/wiki/key-alignment).\n\n## What the beam can represent\n\nThe rigid decoder consumes one slot at every step. The beam keeps several candidate prefixes. At each step it considers accepting the next key slot, or skipping up to its declared limit. A skipped slot is permitted only when it would have generated a repeat of the preceding ciphertext rune under that candidate plaintext.\n\nBeam width controls how many prefixes survive scoring. The skip limit controls which paths can exist at all. These are different bounds: retaining more paths does not introduce a transition that the model forbids.\n\nWe test widths 16 and 64, each with skip limits one and three. Candidates are ordered by cumulative English quadgram score, then lexicographic key-slot path and rune sequence. The final normalized score is reported separately. Because some rune labels contain multiple letters, maximizing cumulative score is not the same as maximizing normalized score. The experiment preserves this declared selection rule rather than changing it after seeing results.\n\n## The complete control grid\n\nThe nine known-reading traces supply their first 240 rune indices, or their full length if shorter. Three seed IDs, two key fixtures and four encoders produce 216 plants. Every plant is decoded with the correct and wrong key using all five decoder configurations: 2,160 results. These reuse source texts and are not independent trials from a population.\n\nThe figures show every correct-key configuration. The complete summary CSV also includes every wrong-key configuration, all of which produced zero exact recoveries and zero accepted scores. That finite result is not a general false-positive rate and does not calibrate a large key search.\n\nSelected counts below explain the figures; the CSV retains all 80 grouped cells and the JSON retains every individual result. Each cell has 27 plants. “Accepted” means normalized score at least −5.5, not a correct answer.\n\n| Encoder and key fixture | Decoder | Exact | Accepted |\n| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |\n| Ordinary addition, either fixture | Every tested decoder | 27/27 | 27/27 |\n| Skipping, single values | Rigid | 1/27 | 2/27 |\n| Skipping, single values | Beam 64 / 3 | 26/27 | 27/27 |\n| Skipping, four-slot runs | Beam 64 / 1 | 0/27 | 0/27 |\n| Skipping, four-slot runs | Beam 64 / 3 | 8/27 | 18/27 |\n| Rewriting, single values | Every tested decoder | 1/27 | 27/27 |\n| Rewriting, four-slot runs | Every tested decoder | 0/27 | 27/27 |\n| Unrelated advance, single values | Beam 64 / 3 | 2/27 | 22/27 |\n| Unrelated advance, four-slot runs | Beam 64 / 3 | 0/27 | 15/27 |\n\n## Why a passing score is insufficient\n\nRewriting leaves much of the original text intact. The score therefore accepts many candidates even though some rune indices are wrong. This is an especially clear example of why “looks like language” and “reproduces the full plaintext” must be recorded separately. The [scorer-language controls](#/experiments/english-scorer-controls) examine another failure mode: meaningful text in some languages can receive a poor English score.\n\nAn admissible true path also need not finish first. In the single-value skip condition with a three-skip beam, every true path is permitted and none is pruned, yet one plant's winning candidate is not exact. A competing retained path scores higher under the declared ordering. The report distinguishes this from structural failure and records the first pruning step if one occurs; no true-prefix pruning was observed in this grid.\n\nAn unrelated advance does not always force failure. If its skipped value happens to satisfy the collision rule, the model can represent it. This explains why some plants in that condition still recover. Conversely, a structurally invalid *recorded alignment* is not a proof that no alternative alignment could spell the same plaintext. Exact candidate recovery is measured independently of the encoder's slot path.\n\n## Even the correct key can be ambiguous\n\nA tiny example makes the issue visible without a language model. Work modulo three with key slots `[0, 0, 1]` and always reject collisions. Plaintext `[0, 1]` emits ciphertext `[0, 1]` using slots zero and one. Plaintext `[0, 0]` emits the same ciphertext by rejecting slot one and accepting slot two. The key and ciphertext alone do not distinguish these two plaintexts under this mechanism.\n\nThe stored encoder trace resolves that ambiguity for verification because it contains the answer's alignment. A solver does not receive that trace. The trace-assisted inversion check is an oracle control, not an available decryption attack.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nDownload this experiment's ZIP and preserve the directory structure. Python 3 standard-library modules are sufficient; no network access, API, external model download or third-party package is required.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/decoder-skip-controls/run.py --check\npython scripts/check_decoder_skip_controls.py experiments/records/decoder-skip-controls/results.json --receipt my-decoder-audit.json\npython experiments/records/decoder-skip-controls/plot.py\n```\n\nThe producer checks every frozen input hash. The independent checker imports no producer functions: it reconstructs source prefixes, generated keys and encoder decisions, replays beam selection, and checks every returned rune sequence and diagnostic. It also recomputes full-text scores using a separate calculation. All 216 plants and 2,160 decoder results passed. Ten small-control tests include exhaustive transition comparisons, long rejection runs, rewrite wraparound, exhaustion, ambiguity, and beam output checked against complete path enumeration. Human review remains pending.\n\n## Scope and next steps\n\nThis is a fresh control inspired by [Dukotah's benchmark work](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/benchmark/README.md), not a replication of that repository's reported percentages. Known readings, including any non-prose material within their selected prefixes, are retained without editing. We do not infer manuscript language, identify its cipher, prove a pad construction, or claim that all skip-aware algorithms share these failures.\n\nA later experiment can change the encoder or alignment rule, but must record those changes and test recovery again. Searching many wrong keys also needs a separate control of the *best score from each entire search*, not just a collection of individual wrong-key scores. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for why the size and selection rule belong in the claim.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/decoder-skip-controls/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "eebe6616369dc24047477cd02783ab9eaa45450afefd643ff0eadb29efe4107b",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "control",
    "label": "Control",
    "description": "Checks a search, decoder or scorer using synthetic inputs or reference text; it does not identify the cipher of an unsolved page."
  }
}

  "related": [],
  "article": "# Can a low-degree polynomial directly generate an LP2 page?\n\n**No, under the exact model tested here.** Every nonempty rune page in archived LP2-00–55 fails a necessary condition for direct polynomial generation of degree at most eight, in both rune-index and prime-value coordinates. The obstruction applies to every integer modulus greater than one, not just a searched list of moduli.\n\nThis says nothing about a polynomial **key** added to unknown plaintext. In that model the polynomial generates only the key, while this test compares its output directly with the manuscript symbols.\n\n## The proposed construction\n\nNumber the retained runes on one page i = 0, 1, 2, … . The tested rule is:\n\n```text\nc[i] ≡ P(N + s*i) (mod m)\n```\n\nHere P has integer coefficients and degree at most eight; N is any integer starting position; s is any fixed integer stride, including negative or zero; and m is any fixed integer greater than one. Coefficients, origin, stride and modulus may differ between pages. The output c[i] is either the rune's zero-based index or its literal Gematria Primus prime value. There is no additional alphabet mapping.\n\n## Why differences can rule out infinitely many parameters\n\nA forward difference subtracts each value from the next. For the squares 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, the first differences are 1, 3, 5, 7, the second differences are 2, 2, 2, and the third differences are 0, 0. Each difference lowers polynomial degree by at least one. A polynomial of degree at most d therefore has zero differences at order d+1.\n\nReducing a sequence modulo m may change those differences from zero into multiples of m. It cannot change the requirement that **m divides every difference at that order**. Consequently, m must divide their greatest common divisor (gcd). If that gcd is 1, no modulus m > 1 can work.\n\nSubstituting N+s*i into a polynomial does not increase its degree in i. This is why arbitrary origins and fixed strides are covered without enumerating them. The proof uses the algebraic form of the rule; it does not estimate a probability.\n\n## A small example you can check by hand\n\n| Sequence | Values | First differences | Second differences | Third differences |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| Squares | 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 | 1, 3, 5, 7 | 2, 2, 2 | 0, 0 |\n| Change only the last value | 0, 1, 4, 9, 17 | 1, 3, 5, 8 | 2, 2, 3 | 0, 1 |\n\nThe modified example has gcd(0, 1) = 1 at order three. It cannot be a quadratic polynomial stream modulo any m > 1 under the stated rule. A gcd other than 1 would merely leave possible divisors to investigate; it would not establish that a polynomial exists.\n\n## Manuscript result and coverage\n\nThe retest uses the repository's archived rune text, retains headings, removes nonalphabet characters, and starts a separate stream for each page. Decimal labels, separators and line breaks do not advance the position. It tests degrees 1–8 separately; constant polynomials are included within every degree bound.\n\n| Coverage | Count |\n| --- | ---: |\n| Page files LP2-00–55 | 56 |\n| Nonempty rune streams | 55 |\n| Representations per stream | 2 |\n| Degree bounds per representation | 8 |\n| Checks with gcd 1 | 880 of 880 |\n\nLP2-50 contains no alphabet runes in this transcription and is explicitly skipped. Its alphanumeric grid is not converted into a rune stream. LP2-56 and LP2-57 are outside the scope.\n\nFor a concrete witness, LP2-00's zero-based rune indices have ninth differences beginning **−1078, 1882, −2478, 1805**. Their successive gcds are 1078, 2, 2, 1. Those four values alone exclude every modulus greater than one for degree at most eight. The downloadable ledger contains all differences and a short gcd-one prefix for each of the 880 checks.\n\n## What would reopen the question?\n\nA polynomial key mixed with plaintext, a higher-degree polynomial, irregularly skipped positions, internal resets, a different rune selection, or an additional output mapping changes the model. Those require their own tests. The result does not eliminate arithmetic ciphers, running keys, recurrences or periodic ciphers as general classes.\n\nThe result is tied to the supplied transcription, not to a new visual audit of every rune. If the transcription changes, rerun the calculation. Agreement between the text and page-JSON versions checks computation and packaging; those versions share their archival source.\n\n## Reproduce and independently check\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP with folders intact, or use the repository. Python 3's standard library is sufficient. No network requests, AI calls or additional packages are needed.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/direct-polynomial-streams/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/direct-polynomial-streams/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command takes successive neighboring differences. The second reads page JSON and computes each difference directly with the binomial-coefficient formula, without importing the first implementation. It also checks 128 synthetic polynomial streams across degrees, moduli, origins and strides, plus the modified-square example above. Both commands must pass.\n\n## Relationship to the earlier archive\n\nThis is a fresh reproduction of the supplied closure register's direct-polynomial claim (C10/C22), using the current published corpus. It is not an original discovery. The earlier archive describes formal Lean checks; this package supplies an elementary proof and independently checked integer calculations, and does not claim to rerun that Lean development. Other entries in the register are not certified by this experiment.\n",

      "caption": "The 86 archived doublets split by intervening mark. Hyphen class includes one pair that also crosses a row wrap; classes are exclusive."

  "article": "# Where the 86 doublets cross a separator\n\nThe standard LP2-00–55 count removes non-runes within each page. That makes some equal runes neighbors in the filtered stream even when a hyphen or row break separates them in the archived text. This audit locates those pairs and tests the site's seven stored LP2 reviewed-text edits.\n\n**Sixty of the 86 pairs are directly adjacent rune characters.** Three have only a row-wrap marker between them, 22 cross a hyphen, and one crosses other punctuation. No doublet crosses an apostrophe alone or with a soft row wrap. These categories are exclusive: a hyphen plus row wrap counts in the hyphen row.\n\n![A bar and legend split the 86 equal-rune pairs by intervening marks: 60 contiguous, 3 row-wrap only, 22 hyphen and 1 other punctuation.](experiments/records/doublet-boundaries/boundaries.svg)\n\n| Intervening marks | Equal pairs | All rune pairs in that class | Rate |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| None: rune characters touch | 60 | 9,637 | 0.623% |\n| Row wrap only (`/`, CR/LF) | 3 | 388 | 0.773% |\n| Apostrophe, perhaps with wrap | 0 | 3 | 0% |\n| Hyphen, perhaps with wrap | 22 | 2,721 | 0.809% |\n| Other separator | 1 | 152 | 0.658% |\n| **All within-page filtered pairs** | **86** | **12,901** | **0.667%** |\n\nThe first three rows follow the site's published rune-token convention: slash row markers and physical line breaks are removed, and an internal apostrophe is allowed. Under that convention, **63 of 10,028 within-token pairs** match (0.628%). This is a transcription-based token definition, not an image-verified judgment that every such pair lies within a manuscript word. Conversely, the 22 hyphen-crossing doublets would disappear from a strictly word-internal doublet count. Rates across these groups are descriptive; the small row-wrap and apostrophe groups do not justify a mechanism claim.\n\n## What the stored corrections change\n\nThe current archive has separate LP2 reviewed-text layers for pages 05, 07, 11, 15, 35, 37 and 38. They alter notation marks but preserve the ordered rune stream. Applying all seven leaves the **86 pair identities and all five doublet category counts unchanged**. None of the stored punctuation changes falls between a doublet in a way that moves it to another class.\n\nThis answers a deliberately limited question. The other LP2 pages have no separate reviewed layer here. The seven layers are not a second complete independent transcription, and this experiment does not recheck 86 pairs against the original 2400×3600 scans. A new rune correction could change both pair identities and counts; a new separator correction could change the word-internal classification without changing 86.\n\nThe [full doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets) explains the 86-event count and provides source coordinates. The [transcription guide](#/wiki/transcription-checking?section=coverage) lists which pages have reviewed layers. The [short-lag profile](#/experiments/doublet-lag-profile) keeps the filtered within-page rule and compares equality at rune distances one through five. These analyses answer different questions.\n\nThe [EA frequency control](#/experiments/ea-frequency-control) asks a separate question: whether the 86 observed repeat positions are numerically plausible as plaintext EA under one exact running-sum equation. It uses decoded GP indices from solved pages rather than assigning English digraphs by eye.\n\nThe [placement audit](#/experiments/doublet-placement) asks whether the event positions cluster by page or sit unusually close together after preserving the number of available within-page edges.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP without flattening folders. Python 3.12 and its standard library suffice:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/doublet-boundaries/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/doublet-boundaries/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer records SHA-256 hashes for the alphabet, all 56 archived page texts, and the seven page records with reviewed layers. `results.json` lists every doublet by page, zero-based rune index, source character offsets, intervening marks and reviewed-layer classification. Run `--write` to regenerate the report and SVG. The independent checker extracts runes with a separate regular-expression path, recounts separator classes, and checks all 86 offsets against the existing source-location ledger. That verifies the archived data handling; it does not authenticate the photographed glyphs.\n",

  "visuals": [

      "path": "experiments/records/doublet-context/context.svg",
      "caption": "All 29 ciphertext symbols at doublet positions, compared with conditional permutation means; ticks are not individual significance thresholds."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# What surrounds the 86 ciphertext doublets?\n\nThe [doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets?section=ea-constraint) describes one proposed equation in which a repeated ciphertext rune would mark a plaintext EA. That statement is easy to overread. It fixes the **plaintext symbol at a transition** under the equation; it does not say that the repeated *ciphertext* rune is the EA rune, or that the neighboring ciphertext runes should spell an English word. This experiment records those local ciphertext values and asks whether they have extra ordering structure under a declared conditional control.\n\n![Counts of all 29 ciphertext symbols at the 86 doublet positions, compared with means from fixed-mask within-page permutations.](experiments/records/doublet-context/context.svg)\n\n## What the equation predicts\n\nFor `Cᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁ + Kᵢ(Pᵢ − 28) mod 29` with nonzero `Kᵢ`, `Cᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁` if and only if `Pᵢ = 28` (EA). The doublet's visible rune is `Cᵢ`, the **current ciphertext state**. It can be any of the 29 runes. A doublet on AE does not make AE the proposed plaintext; a doublet on EA does not offer special confirmation.\n\nIf the *following* plaintext rune is not EA and its key is independently uniform on 1–28, its difference `Cᵢ₊₁ − Cᵢ` is uniform on those 28 nonzero residues. The next ciphertext rune is then uniform over the 28 symbols **other than** `Cᵢ`. It is not independent of `Cᵢ` in absolute symbol terms, because equality is forbidden. If the following plaintext is EA, the next difference is zero and a triple results. The observed doublet mask has no consecutive zeros, so this record cannot use a fixed-mask control to judge how surprising that absence is.\n\n## The actual local inventory\n\nFrom the archived LP2-00–55 text, filter to the 29 GP runes, keep headings, and compare neighbors only within pages. This gives **86 zero differences in 12,901 transitions**. Each event is recorded by page and zero-based rune index in the [result ledger](experiments/records/doublet-context/results.json). One event has no preceding within-page difference; one has no following one. None has a zero difference immediately beside it. The remaining 85 preceding and 85 following differences are tabulated separately in all 28 nonzero residues.\n\nThe event-symbol counts range from **0 to 7**, rather than 3 to 7. GP index 17 (B) has no event; index 25 (AE) has seven; index 28 (EA) has three. The latter labels are ciphertext symbols, not decoded plaintext. Across all 29 bins there are **123 pairs of events sharing the same ciphertext symbol**. The local before-versus-after residue imbalance, defined in the [plan](experiments/records/doublet-context/plan.txt), is **27.786**. Both summaries were selected before this control was run, but the underlying doublet observation had already been seen.\n\n## A control that holds the known anomalies fixed\n\nFor each page, retain its first ciphertext rune, the positions of all zero differences and the multiset of all nonzero differences. Shuffle only the nonzero difference order within that page, then cumulatively add the differences modulo 29 to rebuild a synthetic ciphertext page. This preserves the **86-event mask exactly** and also preserves each page's difference histogram. It asks whether *placement relative to those zeros* adds anything beyond those known properties. It does not simulate English, a key generator, or the chance of obtaining 86 zeros in the first place.\n\n| Diagnostic | Observed | Central 95% of 5,000 conditional permutations | Trials at least observed |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Same-symbol pairs among doublet events | 123 | 108–150 | 2,950 / 5,000 |\n| Before/after difference imbalance | 27.786 | 12.745–34.259 | 854 / 5,000 |\n\nBoth observed values sit inside these conditional ranges. In the figure, blue bars are the complete observed 29-symbol inventory and red ticks are the average count for each bin across the permutations. The ticks are not 29 separate significance cutoffs. The report also includes all 28 before and after residue bins, every event location, the seed (`330122`), and both inclusive rank directions.\n\nThis is **not independent corroboration** of the earlier [nonzero-difference histogram](#/experiments/ea-difference-independence). The same source differences are reused, and the new control deliberately fixes their pagewise histograms. The broad question “are these 86 positions really plaintext EA?” remains unanswered. A proposed key schedule would have to predict something further that can be checked without freely choosing plaintext neighbors after seeing the ciphertext.\n\n## Reproduce and limits\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP without flattening it, then run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/doublet-context/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/doublet-context/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer reruns all 5,000 seeded conditional permutations and checks the saved JSON and SVG byte for byte. The separate checker re-extracts the Runic Unicode block, recomputes all 86 event locations and both diagnostics, and verifies each source hash. This checks the archived text, not a fresh image transcription. Neither the control nor the exact algebra identifies the cipher, and these exploratory ranks are not adjusted for the wider history of questions asked of the same 86 events. See the [boundary audit](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries) and [placement audit](#/experiments/doublet-placement) for other, non-interchangeable scopes.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/doublet-context/article.md",

  }

      "caption": "Lag-three forward differences: all 29 bins, split into within-page and cross-page comparisons. Of the ten +4 matches, three stay within one page and seven cross pages. Brown marks show fixed-event shuffle expectations, not significance thresholds."

  "article": "# Distances between doublet events\n\nThe proposal asks whether repeated runes, extracted in manuscript order, form a patterned sequence of their own. This recount finds **10 forward +4 differences at lag three, out of 83 comparisons (12.05%)**. It does not reproduce the reported 12.9%, and it does not verify the proposed p-value.\n\n“Not supported” refers to reproducing the exact numerical claims with these inputs and rules. It does not mean that every doublet-based cipher has been tested or rejected.\n\n## What is an event?\n\nRead LP2-00–55 in numerical order, including headings. Retain only the 29 alphabet runes within each page. Count overlapping adjacent equal pairs: AAA contributes two A events. Never create an event across a page boundary. Then join the extracted events in page order. The result is 86 events.\n\nAt lag one, compare each event with the next; at lag three, compare it with the event three places later. For example, in an event sequence A, B, C, D, the first lag-three comparison is A to D. This lag measures **event positions**, not rune positions or page distance.\n\nThe [short rune-lag profile](#/experiments/doublet-lag-profile) instead compares positions in the original rune streams before extracting doublets. Its lag-three denominator is 12,791 rune pairs, not the 83 event pairs counted here.\n\nFor indices a and b, the directed difference is `(b-a) mod 29`. The circular distance is the smaller of that difference and its reverse. Thus +4 and −4 share circular distance 4 but occupy different directed bins, 4 and 25. The proposed +4 claim is directional.\n\n## Complete comparison\n\n| Event lag | Comparisons | Cross-page comparisons | Mean circular distance | Forward +4 | Circular distances 5, 12 or 14 |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| 1 | 85 | 41 | 734/85 ≈ 8.6353 | 2 | 31 |\n| 2 | 84 | 63 | 52/7 ≈ 7.4286 | 1 | 22 |\n| 3 | 83 | 75 | 626/83 ≈ 7.5422 | 10 | 14 |\n\nThe earlier proposed lag-one mean was 8.81. These inputs instead give 8.6353. The exact reason for the difference cannot be determined without the original event list and counting implementation. The stored output includes all events and every comparison so a future comparison can locate the first divergence.\n\nPage boundaries matter here: 75 of 83 lag-three comparisons cross them. Resetting the comparisons at page boundaries would answer a different question; it is not an interchangeable implementation detail.\n\n## What should the +4 baseline be?\n\nUnder a uniform shuffle of this fixed event multiset, the exact probability of a forward +4 difference between distinct positions is **8/215 ≈ 3.7209%**. It is not exactly 1/29, because these event symbols have unequal frequencies. For counts c(a), sum `c(a) × c((a+4) mod 29)` over all a and divide by `86 × 85`.\n\nThis probability is an expectation for a single ordered comparison. Multiplying it by 83 gives the expected lag-three count, approximately 3.0884. It is **not** the probability of observing ten or more matches: comparisons share events, and a binomial independence assumption is not justified by this calculation.\n\nNo permutation tail probability is calculated here. Selecting +4, lag three, or the group of distances 5, 12 and 14 after inspecting data introduces selection choices. A later significance test must state which choices it addresses. See [null models](#/wiki/null-models) and [search space](#/wiki/search-space).\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP with its folders intact. No packages, network access or AI service are required.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/doublet-event-lags/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/doublet-event-lags/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer uses the included doublet extractor and prints fresh JSON without `--check`. The independent checker uses overlapping regular-expression matches on the archived rune text, then checks every event, lag pair, histogram, distance and boundary flag. It also computes shuffle expectations from symbol frequencies instead of enumerating pairs of event positions.\n\nThese checks establish agreement about the archived transcription. They do not independently settle ambiguous handwriting. The [doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets) explains the source rules and supplies the original pair coordinates.\n\n## Read and reproduce the figure\n\nThe figure shows every possible forward difference, including bins with zero occurrences. Dark bars count within-page comparisons; pale bars count cross-page comparisons. The ten +4 matches split into **three within-page and seven cross-page** comparisons. These counts have different opportunities: only eight lag-three comparisons stay within a page, while 75 cross pages. Comparing raw bar lengths alone would overlook that imbalance.\n\nBrown marks show the expected total count per bin after shuffling the fixed multiset of 86 events. They are not confidence limits or a cutoff for significance. The chart does not assign separate null expectations to the two boundary groups.\n\nThe SVG is included in the download. To regenerate a figure, install Matplotlib in your Python environment, then run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/doublet-event-lags/plot.py --output my-distribution.svg\n```\n\nThe script refuses to overwrite an existing file. The numerical producer and independent checker still require only the standard library; plotting is optional.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/doublet-event-lags/article.md",

  }
}

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/doublet-lag-profile/profile.svg",
      "caption": "Observed equal-rune pairs (dots) compared with exact page-shuffle expectations (thin marks) and central ranges across 2,000 shuffles (bands)."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Equal-rune pairs at distances one through five\n\nThe 86 neighboring equal-rune pairs are unusual under a count-preserving page shuffle. **The same deficit does not continue through lags 2–5** under this particular reference model. This narrows the observation: it concerns adjacency, rather than a blanket avoidance of repeating a rune within five positions.\n\n## Exactly what was compared\n\nFor each archived LP2-00–55 page, retain the 29 alphabet runes in order, including headings, and remove other characters. At lag *d*, compare rune *i* with rune *i + d* for every position that fits. Pairs may cross a word or line break after filtering; none cross a page boundary. LP2-50 contributes no rune pairs. A lag is measured in **rune positions**, not in the sequence of extracted doublet events used in the [event-lag experiment](#/experiments/doublet-event-lags).\n\n| Rune lag | Equal pairs | Pairs compared | Page-shuffle expected | Central 95% of 2,000 shuffles |\n| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| 1 | 86 | 12,901 | 439.17 | 398–480 |\n| 2 | 435 | 12,846 | 437.29 | 396–479 |\n| 3 | 434 | 12,791 | 435.42 | 396–476 |\n| 4 | 451 | 12,736 | 433.55 | 392–472 |\n| 5 | 463 | 12,681 | 431.68 | 391–469 |\n\n![Five horizontal rows show observed equal-rune pair counts against the page-shuffle central ranges. Lag one is far left of its range; lags two through five lie within theirs.](experiments/records/doublet-lag-profile/profile.svg)\n\nThe dark dot is the observed count, the pale band is the middle 95% of seeded shuffles, and the thin mark is the exact expected count. The band is a visual reference for one shuffle model, not a general confidence interval for possible ciphers. Lag five sits near its upper edge; its 463 matches were met or exceeded in 109 of the 2,000 shuffles. This is not a basis for selecting lag five as a discovery after seeing the chart.\n\n## Why the shuffle expectation changes with lag\n\nFor a page with *n* runes and symbol counts *c*, any pair of distinct positions matches with probability `Σ c(c−1) / [n(n−1)]` after uniformly shuffling that page. A lag *d* supplies `max(n−d, 0)` pairs. Multiply and sum over pages to get the exact expected count shown above. The denominator falls as the lag grows; the expectation therefore changes even when the per-pair shuffled probability is the same.\n\nEach of the 2,000 trials independently permutes the filtered runes **within each page**, preserving the page lengths and rune frequencies. It does not simulate English, a running-sum cipher, or a key process. None of those trials had as few as 86 lag-one matches, but `0/2,000` only bounds what this Monte Carlo run observed. The [uniform additive-key record](#/experiments/uniform-additive-doublets) supplies an exact probability for a different, more restrictive model; its tail should not be transferred to this shuffle model.\n\nThe observed contrast is compatible with several mechanisms: a rule that avoids immediate repeats, a plaintext/cipher relation that makes adjacent repeats rare, or preprocessing that alters adjacent symbols. It does not identify which one applies. Also, lags 2–5 were selected after the adjacency anomaly was known. The shaded bands are descriptive and unadjusted for multiple looks.\n\nThis profile filters out the separators between runes. The [boundary audit](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries) shows that 26 of the 86 adjacent equal-rune pairs have an intervening row wrap or punctuation mark in the archived text.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the experiment download without flattening folders. Python 3.12 and its standard library suffice:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/doublet-lag-profile/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/doublet-lag-profile/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer records SHA-256 hashes of all 56 page texts and the index. Run `--write` to regenerate the stored JSON and SVG. The second script independently extracts Runic Unicode characters with a regular expression, recounts each lag and derives the exact shuffle expectations. The JSON includes exact fractional expectations, shuffle intervals, counts on either side of each observed result, seed and quantile convention. This is a transcription-based analysis; it does not resolve disputed glyph readings in the source photographs. For the complete 86-event ledger and the algebraic EA proposal, see [the doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets).\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/doublet-lag-profile/article.md",

  "article": "# Are the 86 doublets clustered by page or position?\n\nThe low overall doublet count is established for the archived LP2-00–55 rune streams. A separate question is where the 86 surviving equal-neighbor events fall. This record compares their locations with **two explicitly conditional placement controls**, so a short page is not treated as if it offered as many opportunities as a long one.\n\n![Observed zero-doublet pages, page-count variance, shortest event gap and page-edge events shown against length-aware random-placement ranges.](experiments/records/doublet-placement/placement.svg)\n\n| Measurement | Observed | Fixed-total placement: central 95% | Fixed-page-count placement: central 95% |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Pages with no doublet | 13 of 55 | 8–17 | Fixed at 13 |\n| Page-count variance / mean | 1.204 | 0.715–1.483 | Fixed at 1.204 |\n| First or last five within-page edge slots | 4 | 1–8 | 1–8 |\n| Shortest gap between event starts | 6 runes | 1–7 | 1–6 |\n| Median gap | 113 runes | 81–127 | 83–117 |\n| Gaps of five runes or less | 0 | 0–6 | 0–6 |\n\nAn event occupies the left edge index of an equal adjacent rune pair. The input has **12,901 available within-page edges** on 55 nonempty pages; LP2-50 has no alphabet runes. For gap measurements, place the filtered page streams one after another in LP2 numerical order and subtract the starting rune coordinates of consecutive events. The resulting 85 gaps include comparisons across page boundaries, but no *event* is created across a page boundary. The shortest actual gap is six runes, on LP2-27. “Gap” here is a distance between event starts, not the [alphabet distance between extracted doublet symbols](#/experiments/doublet-event-lags).\n\n## Why 13 empty pages is not itself surprising\n\nUnder the first control, choose 86 distinct edge slots uniformly from all 12,901 available slots. This keeps the observed total and the actual page lengths but lets each page's event count vary. Using each page's length, the exact expected number of nonempty pages with **zero** events is **12.25**. Ten thousand seeded placements yielded a central range of 8–17; the observed 13 sits inside. The raw count variance-to-mean ratio is 1.204, likewise inside its length-aware range. Shorter pages have fewer chances to contain an event, so a crude equal-length Poisson comparison would answer a different question.\n\nThe 13 zero-doublet pages are LP2-05, 07, 13, 14, 15, 17, 28, 31, 37, 38, 40, 49 and 53. Their mean rune length is 214, versus about 242 for the 42 pages with at least one event. The complete output lists every page's length, count and event index. This difference in means is descriptive; the length-aware placement result is the relevant control for the zero-page count. No page style or section classification is inferred from these numbers.\n\n## Are neighboring events kept apart?\n\nWith the total-only placement control, the minimum gap reaches six or more in **540 of 10,000** trials. With the second control, which keeps each page's observed doublet count fixed and randomizes only its event positions, it does so in **451 of 10,000** trials. The absence of gaps one through five is therefore near the edge of both reference distributions, while the median gap of 113 and the four events in the first or last five edge slots lie within their central ranges.\n\nThese tail fractions are exploratory. The minimum-gap observation was already known when these controls were chosen, and a uniformly selected set of edge slots does not reproduce every way a rune stream can make overlapping equal pairs. Natural-language EA positions, punctuation policy and a real key schedule could each alter gap behavior. The controls help specify a future mechanism test; they do not identify one.\n\n## Reproduce and extend\n\nExtract the ZIP with its directory structure. Python 3.12 and the standard library suffice:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/doublet-placement/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/doublet-placement/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer stores input hashes, all 86 event slots, page lengths, exact zero-page expectation, simulation seeds, central ranges and inclusive rank counts. The independent checker extracts the runes another way, compares every event to the published [source-location ledger](#/wiki/doublets?section=counts), and recomputes the exact zero-page expectation from binomial coefficients. Run `--write` to regenerate the JSON and SVG. The analysis is conditional on the archived transcription; it does not settle uncertain glyphs or compare an independent complete transcription. For the boundary treatment of these same events, read the [separator audit](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries).\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/doublet-placement/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "1698649fcbfd2086f4870b27e2412677b57cb03e580ffc419a1587550b95d927",

    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }
}

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/differences.svg",
      "caption": "Counts for all 28 nonzero difference residues against the equal-count reference; the chart also reports the adjacent nonzero-difference match count."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Are the nonzero differences independent under the EA-stalling model?\n\nThe [EA-frequency control](#/experiments/ea-frequency-control) compared the 86 LP2 doublets with decoded GP EA on solved pages and examined the index of coincidence (IoC) of successive ciphertext differences. This companion check asks what the **specific independent-nonzero-key version** of that equation predicts beyond the zero count. It keeps the observed zero positions and page boundaries fixed; it does not search for plaintext or keys.\n\nUnder `Cᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁ + Kᵢ(Pᵢ − 28) mod 29`, with each key independently uniform on 1–28 and independent of a fixed plaintext, every plaintext EA gives difference zero. For any other plaintext rune, multiplication by its nonzero offset permutes 1–28. Therefore, **conditional on the zero mask**, the other differences must be independent uniform draws from those 28 residues. This is a prediction of the declared key model, not of every running-sum cipher. A periodic, deterministic or nonuniform key need not have it.\n\n![Counts of the 28 nonzero difference residues on LP2-00–55, with their equal-count reference marked in red.](experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/differences.svg)\n\n## Input and two diagnostics\n\nRead archived LP2-00–55, including headings. Retain the 29 GP runes, discard other characters, and subtract each previous rune index from the next **within the same page** modulo 29. There are 12,901 differences: **86 zero** and **12,815 nonzero**. No pair is formed across a page boundary. The zero mask remains at its observed positions in all simulations.\n\nThe first diagnostic is the Pearson chi-square of the 28 nonzero residue counts against an equal-count reference. The expected count per residue is **12,815 / 28 ≈ 457.68**. The second counts equal neighboring nonzero differences. Both difference positions must be consecutive within one page; a zero between them breaks the comparison. That leaves **12,676 eligible pairs**, with **452.71** expected equalities if the nonzero draws are independent uniform residues.\n\n| Diagnostic | Observed | Central 95% of 2,000 conditional draws | Draws at least observed |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| 28-bin Pearson chi-square | 42.056 | 14.403–43.092 | 69 / 2,000 |\n| Equal neighboring nonzero differences | 432 / 12,676 | 412–492 | 1,685 / 2,000 |\n\nThe histogram statistic is near the high end of this seeded conditional reference. The order-sensitive count sits within it. The simulation uses seed `33012026`; every trial fills only nonzero-mask slots with independent draws from 1–28. In a positive control, those synthetic differences were accumulated into ciphertext and differenced again, recovering the simulated values exactly. The complete result stores all 28 observed bins, both tails of each simulated rank, source hashes and the plan.\n\n## The histogram is not independent evidence from the previous IoC\n\nLet `m = 12,815` and let `c₁ … c₂₈` be the nonzero difference counts. The chi-square is `28 Σ cᵣ² / m − m`. With the **86 zero differences fixed**, the full difference IoC has numerator `86 × 85 + Σ cᵣ(cᵣ − 1) = 86 × 85 + Σ cᵣ² − m` and a fixed denominator `12,901 × 12,900`. Both statistics are increasing functions of the same `Σ cᵣ²`. They rank every conditional simulated histogram in exactly the same order. The histogram makes the individual residues inspectable; its 69/2,000 upper rank is **not a second independent hint** alongside the earlier IoC result.\n\nNeighboring equality instead uses the **order** of nonzero differences. A page can keep every residue count—and thus the chi-square and IoC—while a rearrangement changes this adjacent-pair statistic. Here 432 equalities are below the 452.71 uniform expectation but inside the simulated central range. It would be a mistake to infer a periodic key, or its absence, from this one lag-one check.\n\n## What the result leaves open\n\nThe model and diagnostics were selected after the low doublet count and difference IoC were already known. These inclusive Monte Carlo ranks are descriptive and unadjusted for that selection or for examining two related summaries. They do not provide a prospective probability that the manuscript uses this cipher. A near-uniform residual distribution is compatible with many mechanisms; a small departure would challenge only the independently uniform nonzero-key version under these boundaries and transcription choices.\n\nNo plaintext EA positions have been verified, no key has been recovered, and no unknown page has been read. A deterministic key schedule, a clock that pauses on EA, word or page resets, changed rune mapping, and alternate transcription layers require separately declared tests. See the [doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets?section=ea-constraint) for the algebra and the [placement audit](#/experiments/doublet-placement) for the spatial distribution of the 86 zeros.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract this experiment's ZIP without flattening folders. Python 3.12 and its standard library suffice:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer reruns the 2,000 conditional draws and checks the saved JSON and SVG byte for byte. The independent checker extracts the Runic Unicode block with a different parser, verifies every source hash, recomputes the 28 bins and adjacent statistic, and calculates chi-square from an exact rational formula. Both use archived text, not a fresh manual rereading of the JPEGs. The [test plan](experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/plan.txt), [result data](experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/results.json) and [figure](experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/differences.svg) are available separately.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/ea-difference-independence/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "ed9e118f14945daf3384572e34c4750b1a042de316890a42eb90c05c8b9c0f00",

  }
