      "path": "experiments/records/ea-frequency-control/comparison.svg",
      "caption": "Solved LP1 decoded EA rate and unsolved LP2 doublet rate, each with its own numerator and denominator. Rate similarity is not confirmation of the running-sum model."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Does EA occur often enough in solved text?\n\nThe proposed rule `Cᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁ + Kᵢ(Pᵢ − 28) mod 29`, with every `Kᵢ` nonzero, makes a ciphertext doublet equivalent to a plaintext EA rune at that transition. This is an **exact property of the proposed equation**, not evidence that Liber Primus uses it. A first check is whether its required EA frequency is plausible in text already decoded into Gematria Primus runes.\n\nThe site's solved LP1 controls contain **20 EA runes in 2,782 within-page transition positions** (0.719%). Unsolved LP2-00–55 has **86 doublets in 12,901 within-page positions** (0.667%). If the solved LP1 rate were simply carried over, it would correspond to about **92.7 EA positions** at the unsolved length. That is close to 86, but many different ciphers or text-generation rules can produce the same marginal rate.\n\n![The EA rate in solved LP1 and doublet rate in unsolved LP2 shown as two horizontal bars, 0.719 and 0.667 percent.](experiments/records/ea-frequency-control/comparison.svg)\n\n| Source and measurement | Events | Positions | Rate |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Solved LP1-01, 03–16: decoded GP EA | 20 | 2,782 | 0.719% |\n| Solved LP2-56–57: decoded GP EA | 0 | 178 | 0% |\n| Unsolved LP2-00–55: equal neighboring ciphertext runes | 86 | 12,901 | 0.667% |\n\nThe two solved LP2 pages are short; their zero EA count is not a robust estimate for the much longer unsolved portion. The LP1 pages also differ in section and method from that portion. Resampling the 15 solved LP1 pages 10,000 times gives a descriptive range of roughly **54–132 EA positions** when each draw's rate is scaled to 12,901 positions. This shows how the small control set changes with page mix. It is **not** a predictive interval for unknown LP2 plaintext: the pages are section fragments, not independent random samples from a known common language process.\n\n## Why the spelling conversion matters\n\nThe known-reading source preserves actual decoded **GP rune indices** alongside their literal Latin labels. In all 17 solved control pages, removing row wraps and greedily taking the longest GP labels **within each printed token** reconstructs the stored index sequence exactly. That is a check on this literal source layer, not a license to parse normalized English the same way.\n\nIf all token boundaries are erased first, greedy parsing finds **31 EA labels** across the solved LP1 pages instead of the actual **20 EA runes**. The eleven extras are cross-word `E|A` joins such as `ONE | ALONG` and `STRUGGLE | AND`. The downloaded report lists all eleven. Even inside one ordinary English word, the letters `EA` do not prove the manuscript used the single EA rune: `REACT` could be segmented `R·EA·C·T` or `R·E·A·C·T`. In Gematria Primus, EA has prime value 109, while E plus A totals 67 + 97 = 164. Preserve original rune boundaries when testing a frequency or prime sum.\n\n## What about the difference IoC?\n\nSubtract each within-page ciphertext rune from the next modulo 29. This gives 12,901 differences, including 86 zeros. Their observed index of coincidence is **0.035325**. Under an additional idealized assumption—condition on exactly 86 zero differences, then draw all 12,815 nonzero values independently and uniformly from residues 1–28—the expected IoC is **0.035284**. In 2,000 seeded simulations, the central 95% interval was **0.035249–0.035326**; 54 trials reached or exceeded the observed value.\n\nSo 0.0353 is near the upper edge of this **conditional nonzero-uniform** reference, not a standalone confirmation. The reference was chosen after the zero deficit and IoC were known, and other features and baselines have also been examined. Shuffling the ciphertext runes within pages would change the zero count and ask a different question. Uniform nonzero differences are what independently uniform nonzero keys would imply at non-EA positions for this particular equation; other key schedules can behave differently.\n\nThe [doublet placement audit](#/experiments/doublet-placement) tests a different implication: whether the 86 candidate EA positions have unusual page counts or short gaps under explicit event-placement controls. Those controls also cannot establish a plaintext reading.\n\nThe [nonzero-difference companion](#/experiments/ea-difference-independence) keeps the observed zero positions fixed and checks residue balance and adjacent differences. Its 28-bin chi-square is algebraically the same information as the difference IoC reported above, so the two histogram summaries must not be counted as independent evidence.\n\n## Reproduce and limits\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP without flattening it. Python 3.12 and its standard library suffice:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/ea-frequency-control/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/ea-frequency-control/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer hashes the known-reading extract, alphabet and all 56 unsolved text files. The independent checker recounts decoded EA indices, reconstructs literal labels, verifies the cross-word joins, and recalculates the exact difference IoC. The source extract uses established decoded readings and a documented LP1-10 correction; this experiment is not a fresh image audit. It cannot tell whether the 86 doublets are plaintext EA, nor recover the nonzero key sequence. See [the doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets?section=ea-constraint) for the equation and its assumptions, and the [boundary audit](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries) for where the 86 pairs sit relative to stored separators.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/ea-frequency-control/article.md",

  "article": "# Historical Emerson book-cipher control\n\n## Purpose and what this does not test\n\nA book cipher needs a source edition and counting conventions, not just a book title. This record reproduces the documented 2014 opening-image coordinates against the frozen Emerson Self-Reliance PDF derivative. It gives newcomers a working control and a trace they can inspect before proposing new book-cipher experiments.\n\n**The answer was known before this rerun.** This is a historical replication, not blind discovery, an independent confirmation of source selection, or a decipherment of an unsolved manuscript page. No hidden-service address was visited.\n\n## Frozen plan and prior reconstruction history\n\nThe rerun plan and wrapper were committed as `1f67f70` before this execution. Source files, the existing lookup script and the known result were hashed in the plan. An earlier reconstruction had corrected the treatment of embedded verse after inspecting mismatches: the verse remains inside prose paragraph 36 rather than creating extra paragraphs. That earlier adjustment is disclosed in the existing evidence manifest and is not presented here as a rule discovered independently.\n\nThe PDF is the contemporary snapshot linked in the historical walkthrough. Its hash is fixed, but the original creator's exact edition is not authenticated by this reproduction.\n\n## Counting conventions\n\nRe-extract the pinned PDF with pypdf 6.19.0 in layout mode. Begin at the first prose paragraph, exclude numeric page footers, and use four-space prose indentation to begin paragraphs. Seven-space verse remains in its surrounding paragraph. Apply Unicode NFKC normalization and join wrapped lines according to the stored extraction rule. All 50 extracted paragraphs must match the frozen derivative.\n\nCoordinates are one-based paragraph:sentence:word:letter positions. Sentences split at `.`, `!` and `?`; words split on whitespace with edge punctuation removed; only ASCII letters count inside the selected word. Single-character entries are copied literally. These are the documented reconstruction conventions, not a universal natural-language sentence parser.\n\n## Result\n\nThe complete trace matches the archived control. Fifteen coordinate lookups and seven literal characters reconstruct:\n\n```\nauqgnxjtvdbll3pv.onion\n```\n\nThis is a historical output string. Reproducing it says nothing about any current service at that name. The supported claim is only that these exact inputs and rules reproduce the recorded trace.\n\n## Complete coordinate trace\n\n| Entry | Printed PDF page | Selected word | Output |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| 1:2:3:1 | 1 | always | a |\n| 3:3:13:5 | 2 | genius | u |\n| 45:5:2:3 | 19 | acquires | q |\n| 20:3:20:5 | 9 | among | g |\n| 8:3:8:6 | 5 | action | n |\n| 48:5:14:2 | 20 | experience | x |\n| 21:13:4:1 | 9 | justice | j |\n| 25:1:7:4 | 12 | truth | t |\n| 15:9:3:4 | 7 | above | v |\n| 1:1:16:3 | 1 | and | d |\n| 4:3:3:1 | 2 | being | b |\n| 8:3:26:4 | 5 | daily | l |\n| 47:3:3:5 | 19 | equality | l |\n| 3 | Literal | Copied directly | 3 |\n| 13:2:5:4 | 6 | corpse | p |\n| 1:4:16:4 | 1 | private | v |\n| . | Literal | Copied directly | . |\n| o | Literal | Copied directly | o |\n| n | Literal | Copied directly | n |\n| i | Literal | Copied directly | i |\n| o | Literal | Copied directly | o |\n| n | Literal | Copied directly | n |\n\nThe first coordinate, 1:2:3:1, selects the third word of the second sentence in paragraph 1: `always`. Its first letter is `a`. The JSON output includes each full selected sentence, so a reader can check the counting rather than trusting the final string alone.\n\n## Reproduce from files\n\nUse Python 3.12.10 and pypdf 6.19.0. Install the exact dependency in your preferred environment:\n\n```\npython -m pip install pypdf==6.19.0\npython experiments/records/emerson-book-cipher-control/run.py --check\n```\n\nDependency installation needs package access; the actual experiment makes no network request. The wrapper checks every frozen input hash, invokes the existing reproduction script with `--check-pdf`, compares all 50 paragraphs, and checks the complete output trace. It then compares the new report with the saved one. Missing dependencies or changed inputs fail visibly.\n\nTo save a separate report:\n\n```\npython experiments/records/emerson-book-cipher-control/run.py --output my-emerson-control.json\n```\n\nExisting output files are never overwritten. [Download the complete trace](experiments/records/emerson-book-cipher-control/results.json). [Download the pinned PDF](exports/sources/emerson-self-reliance.pdf) and [paragraph derivative](exports/sources/emerson-paragraphs.json). The [coordinate payload](exports/steganography/opening-2014.body.txt) is the extracted message body; extraction and signature verification are separate steps described in the opening-image guide.\n\nFor a standard-library-only replay of the frozen paragraphs, run `python scripts/reproduce_emerson.py` without `--check-pdf`. That shorter check does not re-extract the PDF and must not be reported as having done so.\n\n## Retest and review\n\nCodex ran the PDF reconstruction and lookup twice on 20 October 2026. Both produced the same 50 paragraphs and identical complete trace. No counting rule or source changed during this rerun. The diagram was generated afterward from the saved first lookup. Human review remains pending, and the lookup implementation is the existing historical reproduction code rather than a newly independent decoder.\n\n## Family and future variants\n\nA different edition, paragraph convention or source text needs a separate variant with the exact change recorded. An attempt to apply a book cipher to an unsolved LP2 page also needs an independently defined source of coordinates and a success criterion. This historical control is useful for checking an implementation; it does not establish that such a transfer has already been tested.\n\nSee [book-cipher conventions](#/wiki/book-ciphers), [Emerson and the historical source](#/wiki/emerson-self-reliance), and [the opening image](#/wiki/opening-2014).\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/emerson-book-cipher-control/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "7de9e9ddc294d4a29b7df1a017dd0c4b77a5a3eae8a10b88d1b851343cded07c",

    "id": "historical",
    "label": "Historical reproduction",
    "description": "Replays a documented historical step with specified source material and conventions."
  }
}

  "article": "## Would our scorer recognize a real answer?\n\nA search can recover meaningful text and still discard it if its scoring rule expects the wrong language. This experiment isolates that last step: give a fixed English four-letter scoring model known text in eight languages, then shuffle the same letters as a control. No cipher or decoder is involved.\n\nThe model accepts all English and French samples in this run, some German, Italian, Portuguese and Spanish samples, and none of the Finnish or Welsh samples. It accepts none of the 7,680 shuffled controls. That is useful separation from these shuffles, but **acceptance is neither English identification nor proof of a decryption**. Rejection also cannot rule out meaningful plaintext in another language.\n\n## Source and scope\n\nThe idea follows the scorer-language investigation in [Dukotah's repository](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/PAPER.md). We pin that revision and reuse its English quadgram count file and −5.5 threshold. We run a new, narrower control on our existing aligned FLORES translations; we do not reproduce the repository's full decoder benchmark or import its conclusions about the unsolved cipher.\n\nThe [language comparison experiments](#/experiments/parallel-languages) ask which reference profiles resemble manuscript statistics. This experiment instead asks what a candidate-selection tool accepts when the input is already known text. There are no unsolved-page inputs here.\n\n## Fixed procedure\n\nDivide each of the eight 1,012-sentence translations into the same eight consecutive sentence blocks: four of 127 sentences and four of 126. Join sentences with spaces. Apply each of two rules: uppercase and retain A–Z only; or uppercase, canonically decompose Unicode, remove combining marks, and then retain A–Z. The second rule folds many accented letters but is not a general transliteration system. Uppercasing can expand characters, such as ß to SS. The report records retained lengths and discarded alphabetic characters for each block.\n\nTake the first 120, 240 and 400 retained letters from every block. These are nested samples, not three independent passages. Aligned sentence blocks preserve source content boundaries, but equal character prefixes do not necessarily end at the same translated idea. Generate 20 deterministic shuffles of each excerpt, preserving its exact letter counts. Keep all 384 original cells and all 7,680 controls; there is no selection by score.\n\nFor each overlapping group of four letters, use log₁₀(count / total model count). An unseen group receives log₁₀(0.01 / total). Average over the length minus three groups. Accept a sample when this average is at least −5.5. This threshold belongs to this model and preprocessing; it is not portable to an arbitrary language scorer.\n\n## All conditions\n\nEach cell below is accepted originals out of eight blocks. Every condition also has 160 shuffles per language; all have zero accepted shuffles. The figure shows individual original scores and the full observed shuffled range, not a confidence interval.\n\n| Language | A–Z 120 | A–Z 240 | A–Z 400 | Folded 120 | Folded 240 | Folded 400 |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| English | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 |\n| Finnish | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 |\n| French | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 |\n| German | 6/8 | 6/8 | 6/8 | 6/8 | 6/8 | 8/8 |\n| Italian | 7/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 7/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 |\n| Portuguese | 5/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 | 6/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 |\n| Spanish | 6/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 | 8/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 |\n| Welsh | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 |\n\n## What this does and does not establish\n\nThis scorer can reject intact language while accepting a different non-English language. A successful candidate therefore needs more than crossing a threshold: a reproducible decoding rule, declared choices, coherent extended output and checks against controls appropriate to the whole search.\n\nThe shuffles preserve single-letter frequencies but destroy order. They are not wrong-key outputs from a specified cipher. Zero acceptances in this finite collection does not imply zero false positives, especially after searching millions of candidates and keeping the maximum. The overlapping sample lengths, reused translations and shared model also prevent treating these cells as independent trials or a general accuracy estimate. Model-training overlap with the benchmark has not been independently excluded.\n\nThis is not decoder recovery power: it bypasses decoding entirely. The completed [planted decoder controls](#/experiments/decoder-skip-controls) separately measure exact recovery and score acceptance under fixed encoder, key and skip rules. The [bounded search-maximum controls](#/experiments/search-maximum-controls) retain the maximum from each complete null search rather than treating individual null strings as equivalent to selected winners. These are separate experiments; neither retroactively turns this scorer-only test into a manuscript decryption test. The [newcomer control walkthrough](#/wiki/first-experiment?section=search-controls) explains how to read them together.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nDownload the experiment bundle and extract it with its directory structure. No network access, API key or third-party Python package is required.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/run.py --check\npython scripts/check_english_scorer_controls.py experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/results.json --receipt my-scorer-audit.json\npython experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/plot.py\n```\n\nThe producer checks every pinned input hash. The independent checker reconstructs the source excerpts and shuffles, calculates scores by counting four-letter groups rather than importing the producer, and checks every decision within an absolute numerical tolerance of 10⁻¹². Both computations passed; human review remains pending. The saved JSON includes excerpts, hashes, seeds, individual scores and normalization diagnostics, so every plotted mark can be traced back to its input.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/article.md",

  "article": "# Are three missing grid primes unusual under fixed shuffles?\n\nThe [directional prime-path reconstruction](#/experiments/grid-prime-paths) finds 191 prime-path occurrences and 46 of 49 possible decimal-prime values in the first characters of LP2-49–51's grid. Three values are absent. This experiment asks a narrower statistical question: **if the same first digits were rearranged without changing their counts, how often would at least three values be absent under the identical path rule?**\n\n![Histogram of missing prime values in two sets of 5,000 shuffled grids; the actual grid has three missing values.](experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/missing-primes.svg)\n\nThe shaded column marks the observed count of three. It is not a fitted threshold or a third control.\n\n## Fixed rule and controls\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/plan.json) was saved with the two controls, four statistics, replicate count and seed before running them. Stack 32 rows of eight first digits in page order. Enumerate all 1,364 four-cell straight directed paths in eight directions, allowing page crossings. Reject paths containing a `4`. Read the four remaining digits as a decimal integer, including leading-zero strings, and test primality. There are 49 possible prime values from four positions over digits 0–3.\n\nEach control repeats this entire fixed calculation 5,000 times:\n\n1. **Global shuffle:** permute all 256 first digits; preserve their overall counts.\n2. **Within-row shuffle:** shuffle the eight first digits independently in every manuscript row; preserve each row's composition and its page location.\n\nBoth destroy some spatial arrangement while retaining different amounts of local structure. Neither is a model of how the manuscript was actually made.\n\n## Results\n\n| Statistic | Observed grid | Global shuffle mean | Within-row mean |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Eligible paths | 1,058 | 1,034.54 | 1,043.22 |\n| Prime-path occurrences | 191 | 189.62 | 191.42 |\n| Distinct prime values present | 46 | 47.75 | 47.75 |\n| Prime values absent | 3 | 1.25 | 1.25 |\n\nAt least three values were absent in **761 of 5,000** global shuffles and **763 of 5,000** within-row shuffles. The inclusive plus-one empirical upper-tail estimates are **15.24%** and **15.28%**. Three missing values are therefore not rare under either declared control. The complete [result file](experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/results.json) retains the histogram and both empirical tails for every predeclared statistic, not just the favorable comparison.\n\nThis does **not** assign a chance probability to the particular names `1033`, `2213` and `3301`: those values were noticed before this test was designed. It does not account for trying other layouts, directions, path lengths, bases or visually selected patterns. It also does not test any decryption. The result weakens an argument from the *number* of missing values under these two nulls; it cannot rule out a construction based on a more specific independently predicted feature.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nDownload the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/grid-prime-path-null.zip), extract it with its directory structure, then run Python 3.12 or later:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/check.py\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe first script reruns all 10,000 control grids from seed `33012026` and checks the saved JSON byte for byte. The second independently enumerates endpoint pairs with a sieve for the observed grid and 24 fixed shuffled examples; it also checks the histogram arithmetic. The chart script checks the SVG against the saved histograms. The bundled [grid export](exports/alphanumeric-grids.json) supplies the 256 first digits, and the report pins its hash. Since the five documented archive-versus-wiki transcription differences affect only **second** characters, the numeric path statistic is unchanged by those five differences. Other unreviewed first-digit errors would require a new sensitivity test.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "8fa798df618ea50bec5a60f3722ae5af7962900d967cf07d7fffd3afb9221ac9",

  "article": "# Directional prime paths: a reproduced count claim\n\nThis record checks a specific observation about the alphanumeric grids on LP2-49–51. It reproduces **191 occurrences of 46 distinct decimal primes**, with **1033, 2213 and 3301 absent** from a 49-value candidate set. “Supported” refers only to that scoped recount. It does not establish deliberate construction, statistical significance or a hidden message.\n\nThe [illustrated grid guide](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) identifies the original pages and their token conventions. The [prime-path guide](#/wiki/grid-prime-paths) explains the reconstruction and comparison with the published occurrence CSV. This experiment packages the inputs, complete output and two independent implementations for reuse.\n\n## Fixed search rules\n\nStack the 32 original rows in page order 49, 50, 51, retaining eight columns. Read four consecutive cells in each of eight straight directions. Paths cannot turn or wrap around an edge, but may cross page boundaries. Reverse directions count separately.\n\nTake the first character of each token. Reject any path containing a 4; do not remove the cell and join its neighbors. Interpret the four-position string as a decimal integer, allowing leading zeroes, and retain it if prime. Then record the four suffix characters and, separately, the base-4 interpretation of the digit string.\n\nFor example, LP2-49 grid coordinates (row, column) `(7,2) → (6,3) → (5,4) → (4,5)` contain `0G → 0S → 0d → 2U`. The digit string is `0002`, the decimal value is 2, and the suffix extraction is `GSdU`. Retaining the path does not make those suffixes plaintext.\n\n## Complete result\n\nThere are 1,364 geometrically valid directed paths. Of these, 306 contain a 4 and are rejected, leaving 1,058 eligible paths. The decimal-prime filter retains 191 occurrences, including 60 with leading zeroes and 40 crossing a page boundary. These counts describe overlapping paths, not independent trials.\n\nThere are 256 possible four-position strings over digits 0–3. Their decimal values include 49 primes; 46 occur in the grid. The three missing strings become 79, 167 and 241 respectively when read in base 4. All three conversions are prime, but that is a separate observation: the original filter tests decimal primality. Only 147 of the 191 retained occurrences are prime under both interpretations.\n\nThe JSON contains every retained path, its tokens, original page coordinates, direction vector, digit string, suffix extraction and both numerical interpretations. Its frequency table includes all 49 candidate primes, including zero counts. No appealing suffix string was selected as a successful decryption.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract this experiment’s ZIP with its directory structure intact. Python 3.12 and the standard library are sufficient; no installation, network call, AI service or key is needed.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-paths/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-paths/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer uses the shared, included `grid_prime_paths.py` helper to enumerate starts and direction vectors from the coordinate-bearing export. Without `--check`, it prints a fresh JSON report.\n\nThe independent checker reads the original archived page records, reconstructs their grid tokens, and enumerates pairs of endpoints instead. It uses a sieve to identify primes rather than the producer’s trial division. It checks the complete set of hits, source coordinates, suffixes, base-4 values and frequency table. Agreement checks the implementations against the same archived transcription; it is not an independent visual reading of every glyph.\n\n## Limits and related variants\n\nChanging to a 16×16 layout, prohibiting page crossings, requiring four nonzero-leading decimal digits, searching longer paths, or requiring both bases to be prime changes the test. Keep such experiments in this family with their changed rules and results visible.\n\nA linked [shuffle-control experiment](#/experiments/grid-prime-path-null) now fixes the path rule and compares the *number* of absent prime values with global and within-row first-digit shuffles. Three or more values were absent in about 15% of each control set. This does not assign a confirmatory probability to the particular three names selected after observation. Shuffling entire tokens would preserve different relationships from shuffling only first characters, and this baseline still does not claim that other representations were exhaustively excluded.\n\nRead [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [null models and selection](#/wiki/null-models) before turning this reproduced pattern into a claim about intention.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-prime-paths/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "eecd104e27f08f7a110538b77a9f475179a6e2801806ced3ada77d911b851942",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "measurement",
    "label": "Manuscript measurement",
    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }
}

  "article": "# Prime paths with manuscript page boundaries\n\nThis variant asks whether the baseline’s exact three-value missing set survives when every four-cell path must stay on a single manuscript page. It does not: **1103 and 3011 become absent as well**. The original absent values, 1033, 2213 and 3301, remain absent.\n\n“Not supported” applies to preserving the same three-value missing set under this change. It does not reject the baseline recount or rule out a cipher.\n\n## The one changed rule\n\nThe [baseline](#/experiments/grid-prime-paths) stacks all 32 rows from LP2-49–51 and permits paths to cross the two page joins. This variant keeps the same row order, columns and coordinate system but rejects a path unless all four cells belong to one page.\n\nEverything else stays fixed: four consecutive cells, eight straight directions, no wrapping or turns, reject any path containing a first character of 4, permit leading zeroes, test primality in decimal, and retain the suffix extraction and separate base-4 value. No cells are deleted or moved.\n\n## Results compared with the baseline\n\n| Measurement | Joined-page baseline | Within-page variant |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Geometrically valid directed paths | 1,364 | 1,148 |\n| Eligible after rejecting digit 4 | 1,058 | 876 |\n| Decimal-prime occurrences | 191 | 151 |\n| Distinct decimal primes | 46 | 44 |\n| Candidate prime values | 49 | 49 |\n| Missing values | 1033, 2213, 3301 | 1033, 1103, 2213, 3011, 3301 |\n\nThe removed set contains 216 directed paths, of which 182 have no digit 4 and 40 pass the decimal-prime filter. The remaining 151 hits equal exactly the baseline’s within-page subset, including their complete source coordinates and extracted strings. The variant produces no new hits.\n\n## Why 1103 and 3011 disappear together\n\nThe baseline has one occurrence of 1103:\n\n```text\nLP2-49 row 10, column 8: 1M\n              page boundary\nLP2-50 row  1, column 8: 15\nLP2-50 row  2, column 8: 0Z\nLP2-50 row  3, column 8: 3Q\n\nForward first characters: 1103\nReverse first characters: 3011\n```\n\nReading those same four cells backward produces the sole occurrence of 3011. Forbidding the boundary crossing removes both. These are two directed hits on one undirected path, not independent locations. This illustrates why counting multiple related observations does not automatically multiply the evidence for an interpretation.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP with its directory structure intact. No external packages or network access are required.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-paths-page-boundaries/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-paths-page-boundaries/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer enumerates starts and direction vectors from the archived grid export. The checker instead rebuilds tokens directly from page records, enumerates endpoint pairs and uses a sieve for primality. Both enforce the same page barrier. The output retains every hit and all 49 candidate frequencies, including zeroes.\n\n## What this comparison establishes\n\nThe exact missing set depends on whether page joins are searchable. Neither convention is proved to be the intended one. Since this variant only removes paths, it cannot restore a value already absent from the baseline; continued absence of the original three is therefore not an independent confirmation.\n\nThis is a deterministic scope comparison, not a statistical test. A chance model would need to preserve or deliberately change the relevant page structure and account for the exploratory choice of statistic. Further changes to layout, path length, numeral base or allowed directions belong in separately declared variants of this family.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-prime-paths-page-boundaries/article.md",

  "article": "# Can image-only detection find every rune row?\n\nThis fixed detector does not reliably recover individual rune rows across the eight selected page layouts. It proposes 83 image bands; 43 match the 65 manually annotated rune rows under the frozen one-to-one interval rule. This is a segmentation control, not evidence of an omitted line in the archive.\n\nThe computation, independent check and visual review are preserved with this experiment. They establish the behavior of this fixed detector on the selected images; they do not certify the transcription.\n\n## What was tested\n\nThe source lead is Dukotah/cicada3301 at revision `f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1`, specifically `liber-primus/analysis/transcription/linecrop.py`. Its row-detection helper operates on the image alone; the later command-line mapping uses canonical rows. We implemented the fixed image-only rule separately rather than executing downloaded code.\n\nThe protocol and manual image reference were frozen before detector execution. The detector examines the central 22–78% of each image. Pixels darker than grayscale 128 contribute to the horizontal projection. A scanline is active when more than 1% of the examined columns are dark. Contiguous active intervals shorter than 20 pixels are discarded before remaining intervals separated by fewer than 12 pixels are merged. No thresholds were tuned after seeing these results.\n\nA proposal matches a reference interval when their intersection divided by their union is at least 0.5. Maximum-cardinality one-to-one matching prevents a large band from counting as several recovered rows. The result retains all eligible edges, matching alternatives and omission controls.\n\n## Results and overlays\n\n| Page | Reference rune rows | Image proposals | Matched rune rows | Overlay |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |\n| LP2-00 | 12 | 12 | 9 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-00.svg) |\n| LP2-03 | 11 | 6 | 4 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-03.svg) |\n| LP2-15 | 8 | 11 | 5 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-15.svg) |\n| LP2-31 | 12 | 12 | 12 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-31.svg) |\n| LP2-39 | 12 | 12 | 9 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-39.svg) |\n| LP2-50 | 0 | 13 | Not applicable | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-50.svg) |\n| LP2-56 | 5 | 10 | 2 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-56.svg) |\n| LP2-57 | 5 | 7 | 2 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-57.svg) |\n\nLP2-50 contains alphanumeric rows in this inventory, not rune rows. It is a non-runic control, not a zero-percent rune-recovery result.\n\nEvery overlay preserves the source JPEG beneath the annotations. Orange R brackets identify reference rune rows, gray N brackets identify other text rows, and blue D rectangles identify image-only proposals. Visual inspection classified all 83 proposals: 43 individual rune rows, 24 non-runic text rows, seven bands spanning multiple rune rows, and nine artwork bands. No reference interval was changed after detection. These categories describe visible regions; they do not identify precisely which pixels caused a merge.\n\nThe numerical count alone is insufficient: LP2-00 has 12 proposals and 12 reference rune rows, yet only nine match. Artwork and merged rows can conceal each other's count discrepancy.\n\n## Omission controls and limits\n\nEach of the 65 reference rune rows is separately treated as absent from a hypothetical candidate inventory while the image and its proposals remain unchanged. The report records whether that row can or must receive a match across all maximum matchings. These are deterministic coverage checks on shared images, not 65 independent trials or 65 actual transcription errors.\n\nAn inventory-only comparison cannot visit a row omitted from that inventory by construction. That comparison illustrates a coverage restriction; it does not reproduce the source repository's classifier or measure its accuracy.\n\nThe pages were selected for different layouts, not randomly sampled. The reference intervals are approximate manual body intervals and prior familiarity with pages is disclosed. Human review remains pending. This experiment does not recognize rune identities, audit within-row insertions or deletions, certify all 75 pages, or show that an archive row is missing.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the reproduction bundle and original-images.zip into the same root, or use the repository. With Python 3 and Pillow 11.3.0, run `python experiments/records/image-row-coverage/run.py --check` from the root. This reproduces the saved results and all eight overlays in a temporary directory and runs the independent check. To retain new output, use `--output row-replay` instead.\n\nFor the individual stages, choose output paths that do not exist:\n\n```sh\npython scripts/test_image_row_matching.py\npython scripts/image_row_coverage.py --output row-results.json\npython scripts/check_image_row_coverage.py row-results.json --receipt row-audit.json\npython scripts/render_image_row_coverage.py row-results.json row-audit.json --output row-overlays\n```\n\nThe producer checks the frozen plan, reference and image hashes. The independent checker uses scalar pixel bytes, regular-expression active runs, rational interval arithmetic and exhaustive matching enumeration without importing the producer. Both use Pillow to decode the JPEGs, so decoding is a shared dependency. The matching unit controls exhaust all 512 bipartite graphs with three vertices on each side.\n\n`results.json` is the untouched first-run report; its status describes the state at computation time. `audit.json` supplies the subsequent independent computational check. `overlay-review.json` records the later visual review and hashes of all eight overlays. Do not edit the first report to imply that review occurred before it was produced.\n\nFuture variants should change one declared segmentation assumption at a time and retain this baseline. More permissive matching alone is not evidence of better row detection.\n\n## Related explanations\n\nSee [transcription checking](#/wiki/transcription-checking?section=coverage-limits) for the difference between a recorded correction and complete review, and [search spaces and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for why a result applies only to the declared test.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/image-row-coverage/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "7b258ffe338acc11039736f852d4850eb5432f668b6c7b692d3af55644b6093c",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "audit",
    "label": "Source or input audit",
    "description": "Checks image provenance, extraction or input coverage against a declared reference; it does not establish a decryption."
  }
}

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/known-reading-languages/controls.svg",
      "caption": "Nearest profile for established English readings under three counting models. All language names have identical styling. A different nearest profile is a limitation of the comparison, not a revised reading."
    }
  ],
  "article": "## Why test readings whose language is already known?\n\nA language comparison should be checked on Liber Primus itself, not only on ordinary translated web text. This control uses **all nine documented reading sections, spanning 17 runic pages**. Their English readings are reproduced with the existing fixed cipher parameters before any statistical comparison. The method is not asked to discover their plaintext.\n\nThe result is useful precisely because it is imperfect: **the pooled readings rank closest to English in every tested representation, but several individual sections have a different nearest language profile.** A nearest statistical match is not a dependable language label for a short section.\n\n## What was fixed before scoring\n\nThe original plan selects every documented section and the pool, includes headings, and uses the same eight FLORES development-language profiles and length-distance definition as the [baseline](#/experiments/parallel-languages). Within each section, page text is concatenated in order and slash/newline wraps are removed. Sections remain separate when their token lists are pooled.\n\nWe compare the literal Latin rune labels using the three corpus representations: letters, accent-folded letters, and GP-style grouping. We also compare native rune-token lengths with each corpus representation. Expanding a rune label into letters changes the counting unit: TH can be two letters but one rune. GP grouping is still a mechanical orthographic sensitivity, not a validated phonetic conversion.\n\n## An input problem found in the first run\n\nLP2-56's published literal field includes its hexadecimal target. A general letter tokenizer interprets the hash's letter fragments as extra words. The unfiltered field produces **50 apparent tokens**, while the rune-derived prose has **25**. All **38 excluded non-rune alphabetic characters** in this control come from LP2-56. The other eight sections have none under the same rule.\n\nWe retained that first report and froze a separate amendment before calculating the amended results. For every section—not just LP2-56—the added comparison constructs Latin labels from the verified decoded rune trace, preserves nonalphabetic delimiters, and replaces any alphabetic source character that is not a GP rune with a separator. This gives a consistently defined rune-derived text profile. The original unfiltered results remain in the download as a diagnostic, not a clean prose-language control. The amendment was made after inspecting the first run and is not described as part of the original predeclared design.\n\n## Reading the results\n\nThe chart names the nearest language profile for each known-English section. Every language uses identical styling. Its first column compares rune-derived letter lengths with corpus letter lengths; the next uses GP grouping on those labels; the final compares native rune lengths with the GP-grouped corpus. The raw report also contains the accent-folded and additional unit-comparison results.\n\n- The pool contains **739 native rune tokens** and ranks closest to English in all nine comparisons. It is still much shorter than the 2,896-token unsolved target.\n- The second koan has 87 native tokens. Its letter profile ranks closest to English, but its GP-grouped and native-rune profiles rank closest to a different candidate. The established English reading has not changed; the counting model has.\n- The final parable has only 20 native tokens. Its nearest profile changes between letter, GP-label, and native-rune representations.\n- For LP2-56, removing hash fragments changes the literal-profile result. This illustrates an input-selection effect rather than new evidence about the plaintext language.\n\nThese results do not prove that the corpus method is useless. They show what its successful pooled comparison does and does not establish. None of the nine sections is a random draw, the pool reuses them, and the representations reuse the same text. Do not turn these outcomes into an independent-trial accuracy estimate or a posterior probability for the unsolved manuscript.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nDownload this experiment's bundle and extract the folder structure intact. It contains the corpus references, archived traces, source transcriptions, reading parameters, original plan, amendment, diagnostic report, current report and scripts. Python 3 standard library only; no API or network.\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/known-reading-languages/run.py --check\npython scripts/check_known_reading_language_control.py experiments/records/known-reading-languages/results.json\n```\n\nThe replay first reproduces the literal readings exactly against the stored page records. The independent checker reconstructs profiles from the separately archived CSV traces and a regex tokenizer; it checks all **70 profiles and 90 rankings** using exact rational distances, and verifies the excluded-character counts. This is computational review, not human review or a new authentication of the readings.\n\n[Current results](experiments/records/known-reading-languages/results.json) · [Original diagnostic](experiments/records/known-reading-languages/diagnostic-original.json) · [Original plan](experiments/plans/known-reading-language-control.json) · [Amendment](experiments/plans/known-reading-language-control-amendment.json)\n\nSee [known readings](#/readings), [word-length conventions](#/wiki/word-lengths), and the [shorter aligned-passage controls](#/experiments/parallel-language-blocks). The [equal-token control](#/experiments/target-sized-languages) now checks reference samples of exactly 2,896 tokens. It does not lengthen these known-reading sections or turn them into independent trials. Genre-matched parallel material and per-section unsolved analysis remain separate work.\n\nFLORES translations and this derived account are provided under CC BY-SA 4.0; source attribution is included in the bundle. Manuscript/source provenance remains documented separately in the page records.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/known-reading-languages/article.md",

  "visuals": [

      "path": "exports/figures/literal-prime-affine.svg",
      "caption": "Two anchor outputs reduce the infinite modulus range to one identity branch and finitely many divisibility candidates."

  "article": "## What was tested\n\nCan one fixed rule `(a × p + b) mod m` rearrange all 29 Gematria Primus prime values into a different ordering of the same values? Here p is the literal prime, not a rune index. Every output must belong to the same prime alphabet, and distinct inputs must give distinct outputs.\n\nFor **every integer modulus m greater than 109**, the only resulting permutation is the identity: each prime stays itself. This is a fresh reconstruction of the supplied research archive’s C07 claim, not a new discovery or a rerun of its original certificate. No manuscript page or proposed plaintext is used.\n\n## Results\n\n| Check | Result |\n| --- | --- |\n| Distinct images of inputs 2 and 3 | 29 × 28 = 812 choices |\n| Exact integer permutations without modular wrapping | One: a=1, b=0 |\n| Remaining anchor choices | 811 |\n| Candidate maps requiring modular checks | 13,212 |\n| Nonidentity full-alphabet permutations | None |\n\nThis does not exclude shifts modulo 29 on **rune indices**, prime-derived running keys, or position-dependent transformations. It is specifically about a single affine map of the full literal-prime alphabet.\n\n## Why the infinite range is finite to check\n\nLet u be the output of 2 and v the output of 3. Subtract their congruences:\n\n```text\n2a + b ≡ u (mod m)\n3a + b ≡ v (mod m)\na ≡ v − u (mod m)\nb ≡ 3u − 2v (mod m)\n```\n\nNo modular division is needed. Composite moduli and coefficients that are not invertible modulo m are included. For each u,v define the unreduced integer expression `L(p)=u+(p−2)(v−u)`.\n\nIf L sends every prime into the palette as ordinary integers, its nonzero slope makes it injective. Exhaustive anchor checking finds only L(p)=p in this branch. Otherwise choose a palette input p whose integer image L(p) is outside the palette. To obtain an allowed modular output y, **m must divide the nonzero integer L(p)−y**. Enumerating those divisors for all 29 possible targets gives every candidate modulus for that anchor pair.\n\nThe identity works for every m>109 because all primes are canonical residues. Every other branch has a nonzero divisibility witness, so it is finite. There is no unsearched large-modulus tail. The report lists every anchor, witness and candidate modulus.\n\n## A worked branch\n\nSuppose 2 maps to 3 and 3 maps to 5. Then L(p)=2p−1, so L(5)=9 is outside the palette. For any allowed output y from 2 through 109, the nonzero difference 9−y has absolute value at most 100. No modulus above 109 can divide it. This anchor pair therefore has no candidates.\n\nOther pairs have larger differences and require checks. The program applies the reduction to every pair; this example alone is not the proof of the complete result.\n\n## Where the conclusion stops\n\n| Relaxed assumption | Counterexample | Consequence |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Drop injectivity | a=0, b=2, m=110 maps every prime to 2 | Output membership alone does not force identity |\n| Use a partial palette | a=109, b=5, m=110 swaps 2 and 3 | The subset {2,3} has a nonidentity permutation |\n\nThe subset example is not a result about any actual manuscript page. A page using fewer than all 29 symbols requires its own support-specific test. Neither counterexample recovers plaintext.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the experiment bundle with its folders intact:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/literal-prime-affine/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/literal-prime-affine/check.py\n```\n\nBoth commands use Python’s standard library and make no network or AI requests. The first reconstructs the full report. The second does not import the producer: it checks candidate completeness by scanning each witness’s bounded modulus range directly, then enumerates all coefficient pairs for moduli 110 through 125. Those sixteen controls check the implementation; coverage above them comes from the divisibility argument, not extrapolation. The checker also verifies the two counterexamples.\n\nBoth checks passed on 20 October 2026. The question, planned procedure and controls are in `plan.txt`. No search bounds, scoring rules or exceptions were changed after seeing the result. Source alphabet, scripts and output hashes are included in the record. Computational review is complete within this scope; human review is pending. No Lean or other proof-assistant build is claimed.\n\nSee [rune indices and prime values](#/wiki/rune-values), [prime indices](#/wiki/prime-indices), [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants), and [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) before applying this result to another proposal.\n\nThe [completed page-support variant](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine-pages) checks the actual archived LP2 supports. It retains two additional LP2-55 maps, illustrating this distinction with manuscript data.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/literal-prime-affine/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "fba95b035e557f3bba7df7d2a8e7195415caa145da5dd06e01c63ee251c7f94d",

    "id": "alphabet",
    "label": "Alphabet-wide analysis",
    "description": "Studies a declared mathematical mapping over the alphabet, rather than decoding an unsolved page."
  }
}

  "article": "## What changes from the baseline?\n\nThe [baseline](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine) requires one affine map to permute the entire 29-prime alphabet. This variant uses the prime values actually present on each archived LP2-00–55 page. Outputs may be any of the 29 allowed primes, but distinct observed inputs must still have distinct outputs. A page may use its own fixed coefficients and modulus.\n\nThe modulus range remains **every integer m greater than 109**. We do not score English or select a proposed reading. The supplied archive’s C08 claim predicted two LP2-55 exceptions; the fresh calculation retained all survivors rather than filtering for that prediction.\n\n## Results\n\n| Archived page support | Pages | Candidate maps checked per distinct support | Nonidentity maps |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| All 29 prime values | 53 pages | 13,212 | None |\n| 28 values, missing 7 | LP2-49 | 14,901 | None |\n| 25 values, missing 7, 29, 59, 103 | LP2-55 | 14,901 | Two |\n| No rune values | LP2-50 | Not tested | No conclusion |\n\nThus **54 of the 55 nonempty rune pages allow only identity** under this exact model. LP2-55 has two additional maps. LP2-50 contains the alphanumeric panel rather than a rune stream; this procedure does not interpret its characters as GP runes.\n\nThe counts refer to distinct input supports, not a separate rerun for each of the 53 identical full-support cases. There are 43,014 candidate-map checks across the three supports. The all-modulus identity branch is handled separately.\n\n## The two LP2-55 exceptions\n\n| Coefficients (a, b, m) | Image of prime 2 | Images of observed odd primes |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| (58, 57, 114) | 59: rune label T | Unchanged |\n| (102, 101, 202) | 103: rune label Y | Unchanged |\n\nBoth have the form `a=m/2+1`, `b=m/2`. For an odd prime p,\n\n```text\nap+b = p + (m/2)(p+1) ≡ p (mod m)\n```\n\nbecause p+1 is even. At p=2, the result is `2+m/2`: 59 for m=114 and 103 for m=202. Each map therefore changes only F to T or Y on this page. It does not decode the remaining runes or recover word boundaries.\n\nNeither 59 nor 103 occurs in LP2-55’s observed input support. Sending 2 to either value therefore does not collide with another observed input. On the full alphabet, the odd input 59 or 103 is fixed too, so two inputs would have the same output. That is why these exceptions do not contradict the baseline.\n\nThe coefficients 58 and 102 are not units modulo 114 and 202 respectively: each gcd is 2. Requiring the affine map to be invertible on the entire residue ring would discard them. Our stated model requires injectivity only on the observed prime support, so they must be retained.\n\n## Complete enumeration without a modulus cutoff\n\nEvery nonempty page support contains primes 2 and 3. Assign distinct allowed images u and v to them, giving 812 anchor choices per support. These determine `a=v−u` and `b=3u−2v` modulo m.\n\nFor each pair, examine the unreduced expression `L(p)=u+(p−2)(v−u)` on the page’s support. If every integer output is already allowed, record that branch separately. In this dataset the only such branch is identity. Otherwise choose the first supported prime whose L(p) is outside the full palette. Every valid modulus must divide one of the nonzero differences `L(p)−y`, where y is an allowed target prime.\n\nThe script tests every resulting divisor above 109, requiring both allowed outputs and no collisions on the observed support. The complete report retains each anchor’s witness and candidate list, the two surviving maps and their full outputs, and every page’s source hash. There is no arbitrary upper modulus bound.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract this variant’s bundle with its folders intact:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/literal-prime-affine-pages/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/literal-prime-affine-pages/check.py\n```\n\nPython’s standard library is sufficient. The bundle includes the baseline’s divisor helper and all 56 archived page texts. No network or AI requests are made.\n\nThe independent checker does not import the producer or divisor helper. It reconstructs page support by counting each alphabet symbol, verifies page hashes, enumerates the possible moduli directly within each witness’s mathematical bound, and checks every survivor. It also verifies that both LP2-55 exceptions fix all its odd input primes and move 2 to a previously absent value.\n\nBoth commands passed on 20 October 2026. The method and controls were recorded in `plan.txt`; no input boundaries, candidate criteria or modulus bounds were changed after inspecting the result. Human review is pending. This is an elementary calculation with a checked certificate, not a proof-assistant build or a new decipherment.\n\n## Limits\n\nThe result concerns the archived rune transcription and one fixed literal-prime affine map per page. It does not cover corrected symbol streams that change a page’s support, position-dependent transformations, noninjective maps, nonlinear rules, rune indices modulo 29, or prime-derived keystreams. A change in any of those assumptions requires a separate variant.\n\nSee [rune values](#/wiki/rune-values), [the full-alphabet baseline](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine), and [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for the distinction between checking a model completely and claiming a general decryption.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/literal-prime-affine-pages/article.md",

  "article": "## What was tested\n\nSuppose a rune is replaced by its Gematria Primus prime value: F becomes 2, U becomes 3, and so on through the 29-value alphabet ending at 109. Could one fixed quadratic formula rearrange that entire alphabet without producing any values outside it?\n\nWe tested `f(x) = ax² + bx + c (mod m)` for **every integer modulus m greater than 109**, requiring all 29 output values to be distinct members of the same prime alphabet. The result is identity only: under these assumptions, each prime must map back to itself.\n\nThis is a replication of the quadratic claim in the supplied research archive. The earlier scripts and reported result were inspected before the plan was written. It is not a new discovery or a blind test. A fresh enumerator and a separately implemented checker agree; human review remains pending.\n\nThis extends the [full-alphabet affine experiment](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine) by allowing a quadratic term. It does not extend the result to every arithmetic cipher. In particular, a changing key added to plaintext has a different equation and is outside this test.\n\n## Why an infinite range can be checked\n\nTrying moduli up to a convenient maximum would leave every larger modulus unresolved. Instead, three chosen inputs restrict which moduli can work.\n\nCall the prime alphabet S. The images of 2, 3 and 5 must be three different members of S; write them as u, v and w. There are `29 × 28 × 27 = 21,924` ordered choices. These three images determine the following integer expression:\n\n```text\nQ(x) = 2u(x−3)(x−5) − 3v(x−2)(x−5) + w(x−2)(x−3)\n```\n\nFor any polynomial fitting those three images, `6f(x) ≡ Q(x) (mod m)`. The factor 6 matters: it cannot simply be cancelled when the modulus is divisible by 2 or 3.\n\nFor each choice of u, v and w, find the first alphabet value x for which Q(x) is not six times an alphabet value. If the final output is some y in S, then m must divide the **nonzero integer** `Q(x) − 6y`. A nonzero integer has only finitely many positive divisors. Taking the divisors for all 29 possible y therefore gives a complete finite list for this branch, including moduli larger than a guessed search cutoff.\n\nThe downloaded certificate records each branch's three images, the chosen witness x, its Q(x), and every candidate modulus. For each candidate the scripts recover all possible coefficients and check the entire output alphabet directly.\n\n## The branch without a finite witness\n\nExactly one choice escapes that divisor reduction: `(u,v,w) = (2,3,5)`. In this branch Q(x) is exactly 6x as an integer, so a different argument is needed. All its possible maps have the form\n\n```text\nf(x) = x + a(x−2)(x−3) (mod m), with 6a ≡ 0 (mod m).\n```\n\nFor every integer x, `(x−2)(x−3)` is either 0 or 2 modulo 6. The only possible changes from identity are therefore a shift by 2a; the input 7 already tests that shift. If it is nonzero, its circular distance from zero is m/3. But two members of this alphabet differ by at most `109−2 = 107`. A valid nonidentity map in this branch would consequently need `m ≤ 321`.\n\nThe checker directly scans the coefficient residues for all moduli 110 through 321. None gives a nonidentity permutation of the alphabet. The argument above handles every larger modulus; those larger moduli are not silently dropped.\n\n## Results\n\n| Finite branches | Candidate-modulus checks | Coefficient checks | Surviving maps |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Modulus coprime to 6 | 261,346 | 261,346 | 0 |\n| Modulus divisible by 2 or 3 | 2,420,451 | 7,993,284 | 0 |\n\nThese counts are branch checks: a modulus can occur under several different choices of anchor images. They are not counts of distinct modulus values across the whole experiment.\n\nThe separate identity-anchor branch contains 318 coefficient expressions representing identity within the checked interval. **Different coefficients need not mean a different function.** For example, modulo 110,\n\n```text\n55x² + 56x = x + 55x(x+1) ≡ x.\n```\n\nThe product x(x+1) is always even, so the extra term is divisible by 110. Reporting that quadratic coefficient as a nonidentity solution would be a mistake.\n\n## Where the conclusion stops\n\nThe requirement to preserve the **whole** alphabet is essential. On only the three inputs `{2,3,5}`, the quadratic `22x² + 16x + 10 (mod 127)` swaps 2 and 3 and fixes 5. However, it sends 7 to 57, outside the prime alphabet. A smaller observed alphabet can therefore permit maps excluded by the full-alphabet test. See the [affine page-support variant](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine-pages) for a separate example of why page-level scope matters.\n\nInjectivity is essential too: the constant function f(x)=2 always stays inside S, but destroys the distinctions between runes. Working with rune indices instead of their literal primes changes the domain. Higher-degree formulas, word-dependent operations, varying coefficients, and polynomial key sequences combined with unknown plaintext are also outside this experiment.\n\nNo candidate plaintext was scored. There was no selection of words that happened to look meaningful, and no claim about the language of the unsolved pages follows from this result.\n\n## How to reproduce it\n\nUse Python 3 with its standard library. No network service or model is needed. From the repository root, choose output filenames that do not already exist:\n\n```sh\npython -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_quadratic_palette.py\npython scripts/run_quadratic_palette.py --output quadratic-certificate.json\npython scripts/check_quadratic_palette.py quadratic-certificate.json --receipt quadratic-audit.json\n```\n\nThe first command compares both coefficient solvers against every coefficient triple for moduli 2 through 18, including cases where division by 6 is invalid. It also checks divisor generation and the scope counterexamples above.\n\nThe producer scans divisor pairs up to the square root and solves congruences using modular inverses after accounting for the greatest common divisor. The checker imports none of that code: it reconstructs divisors by prime factorization and obtains coefficient solutions by lifting a congruence to integer equations. It then checks every finite branch and the bounded identity branch against the saved certificate. The receipt identifies the certificate and checker by SHA-256.\n\nAgreement between these implementations supports the computation. The all-modulus conclusion additionally depends on the reduction explained above. It has not been presented as a proof-assistant result or as completed human review.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/literal-prime-quadratic/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "5aca7221cf7857cdced38d4cd595bbce6725d00bfb416f77fb354957c1886186",

    "id": "alphabet",
    "label": "Alphabet-wide analysis",
    "description": "Studies a declared mathematical mapping over the alphabet, rather than decoding an unsolved page."
  }
}

  "article": "# Does preserving each section change the column-balance result?\n\nThe fixed 464-word arrangement remains unusually flat under a null that shuffles word lengths only within their original four sections. All original section slots and the continuous sixteen-column layout are preserved. This is a sensitivity variant of `lp1-word-length-balance`, not an independent discovery.\n\n| Quantity | Unrestricted baseline | Within-section variant |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| Observed integer score | 128256 | 128256 |\n| Observed column-mean variance | 501/13456 | 501/13456 |\n| Observed variance / model expectation | 0.25150357 | 0.25209625 |\n| Null trials | 49,999 | 49,999 |\n| Trials at or below observed, including ties | 54 | 88 |\n| Plus-one lower-tail estimate | 0.0011 | 0.00178 |\n\nThe constrained expectation is calculated separately. Its exact expected integer score is `612019253902976/1202967183`, and expected column-mean variance is `4781400421117/32374252828896`. The unchanged observed variance divided by that expectation is `1205373117366/4781400421117`.\n\nThe four sections contain 45, 124, 208 and 87 words. Their boundaries do not reset the column position. The report preserves every section's slot counts in all sixteen columns, exact expected column sums and variances, and all 49,999 null scores. A singleton-section boundary and unequal section sizes are covered by small exhaustive controls.\n\n## What changes between the two models?\n\nThe baseline permits any word length to move to any of the 464 slots. This variant permits a word length to move only to a slot in its original section. The lengths themselves, section order and observed arrangement remain unchanged. A section may occupy different numbers of slots in different columns, so keeping its slots matters as well as keeping its histogram.\n\nThe slot diagram shows those fixed memberships. Colors identify the four sections, not high or low word lengths. The same word may have several interchangeable positions within its color. A single section boundary can cut across a row; the next section continues at the next column.\n\nThe two histogram panels use identical integer-score bins, displayed on a common column-mean variance scale. The dashed line is the unchanged observed variance. Lower variance means more similar column means. Every one of the 49,999 null scores per model contributes to its panel; the complete bin counts are downloadable as CSV. The shared seed number does not pair individual trials because the procedures consume random choices differently.\n\n## Why the expectation changes\n\nUnder unrestricted shuffling, every slot samples the same pool of lengths. Under within-section shuffling, each slot samples only its section's pool. The four pools have different means and variances. Columns also contain different section slot counts. Consequently, their expected sums need not be identical, even though every column still contains 29 words.\n\nFor section size N, population variance v and c slots in one column, its sum contributes variance `c*(N-c)*v/(N-1)`. Contributions from independently shuffled sections add. The expected squared distance from the fixed overall mean also includes the difference between each column's expected sum and the overall mean. The script uses exact fractions; the checker obtains the same expectation through pairwise position moments. The ratio in the table therefore uses each model's own expectation.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP with folders intact, or use the repository. Python 3 standard library is sufficient. Run `python experiments/records/lp1-section-balance/run.py --check` to reproduce all constrained scores, run the independent checker and verify the figures. Use `--output section-replay` to retain new files in a new directory.\n\nThe individual stages can also be run from the root with new output paths:\n\n```sh\npython scripts/test_lp1_section_balance.py\npython scripts/lp1_section_balance.py --output section-results.json\npython scripts/check_lp1_section_balance.py section-results.json --receipt section-audit.json\n```\n\nThe [protocol](experiments/plans/lp1-section-balance.md) was committed before constrained shuffles were generated. The producer uses the hashed word ledger and source dependencies. The checker independently scans the original archived text, verifies all 464 words, reconstructs every permutation with explicit index swaps, and calculates the expectation through position-pair second moments. It imports no producer code. Both implementations share Python's pseudorandom primitive.\n\n## Interpretation and publication status\n\nBoth estimates are below the predeclared 0.05 threshold. Preserving section-level length distributions does not remove the low-variance result in this fixed test. The two tests share the same selected arrangement; their p-values must not be combined as independent evidence. The original exploration is not included in either null. Neither model preserves sentence syntax, and neither tests a grille, carrier text, authorial intent or a decryption.\n\nHuman review remains pending. Saved results and the independent receipt are preserved here without overwriting the original baseline. The figures and histogram CSV are generated from those saved reports; the baseline distribution is reused from its published record, not simulated as part of this variant.\n\n## Related explanations\n\nSee [the unrestricted baseline](#/experiments/lp1-word-length-balance), [word-length conventions](#/wiki/word-lengths), and [null models and selection](#/wiki/null-models). The [section-order variant](#/experiments/lp1-section-order) now searches all 24 orders with matching selection in every control. Preserving sentences remains a separate, untested constraint.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp1-section-balance/article.md",

  "article": "# LP1 column balance after searching section orders\n\nThis variant belongs to the LP1 word-length and column-balance family. Human review remains pending.\n\n## What was tested\n\nThe original 464-word sequence fills a table of 29 rows and 16 columns. Its column totals are unusually similar under the previously declared shuffle controls. This variant asks whether that comparison changes when a solver may rearrange the four intact sections and keep whichever arrangement has the most similar column totals.\n\nThe sections are Warning (45 words), Welcome (124), first koan (208), and second koan (87). Word order within each observed section remains unchanged. Every arrangement fills the table continuously, without resetting at section boundaries. The score is `Q = sum((16 * column_total - 1796)^2)`; lower scores mean more balanced columns.\n\nThe [protocol](experiments/plans/lp1-section-order.md) was committed before calculating the order search. It disclosed the already-known fixed-order results. Each of 49,999 controls shuffles lengths within the original sections, searches the same 24 orders, and retains its minimum. It would be unfair to search the observed data but compare that selected result with controls given only one arrangement.\n\n## Results\n\nNo alternative order improves the original score, **128256**. Four orders tie for that minimum because they are cyclic rotations of the original arrangement.\n\n| Representative order | Score Q |\n| --- | ---: |\n| Warning → Welcome → first koan → second koan | 128256 |\n| Warning → Welcome → second koan → first koan | 295680 |\n| Warning → first koan → Welcome → second koan | 257280 |\n| Warning → first koan → second koan → Welcome | 407296 |\n| Warning → second koan → Welcome → first koan | 215808 |\n| Warning → second koan → first koan → Welcome | 337664 |\n\nEach row represents four cyclic rotations with exactly the same score. Rotating the 464-word sequence shifts its sixteen column totals without changing their balance, since 464 is divisible by 16. Thus the 24 arrangements form six classes; this does **not** make the six scores independent.\n\n**440 of 49,999 controls** have a selected minimum no greater than the observed minimum, ties included. The plus-one estimate is `(440 + 1) / 50000 = 0.00882`. The fixed-order within-section comparison was `0.00178`. The larger estimate reflects the extra opportunities given to every control, even though the observed minimum did not improve.\n\nThe result remains below the protocol's 0.05 threshold. It describes this precise word sequence, table width, score, shuffle model and section-order search. It does not estimate the probability of intentional design, provide a decryption, or correct for the wider exploration that originally selected the 464-word object and sixteen-column layout. The two estimates use the same shuffled sections and are not independent evidence.\n\n## Verification and reproduction\n\nThe independent checker reconstructs the source tokens, generates permutations through explicit index swaps, and computes all 24 scores in every control using section-column accumulation. It does not import the producer. It checks **1,199,976 null order scores**, all observed orders, every minimum and tie list, and the full tail count. Every baseline-order control score also matches the earlier section-preserving report. Both implementations share Python's pseudorandom primitive.\n\nThe toy tests exhaust small section permutations with unequal section sizes and repeated values. A non-divisible example demonstrates why the cyclic reduction requires complete rows.\n\nFrom the repository root, choose new output paths:\n\n```sh\npython scripts/test_lp1_section_order.py\npython scripts/lp1_section_order.py --output order-replay.json\npython scripts/check_lp1_section_order.py order-replay.json --receipt order-replay-audit.json\n```\n\nThe producer checks the frozen input hashes. Compare the replay report's SHA-256 with `report_sha256` in the independent audit receipt. The downloadable result retains the full order mapping, observed scores, all six class scores for every trial, and all minimizing orders; none of the searched arrangements is omitted from that representation.\n\n## Read the figures\n\nThe order diagram lists all 24 arrangements in six groups. Every arrangement in one group has the same Q; the bar represents that shared score. Letters label sections, not rune values. The histogram shows the minimum score retained from every complete 24-order search. Its vertical scale counts trials, and its dashed line is the observed minimum. All 49,999 trials are included; the bin counts are downloadable as CSV.\n\n## Run the complete reproduction\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP with folders intact. Run `python experiments/records/lp1-section-order/run.py --check` from its root. Python 3 standard library is sufficient; the run is offline. Use `--output order-replay` to retain results in a new directory. The wrapper repeats the simulation, independently checks every order score, and reproduces the figures and histogram.\n\nSee the [fixed-order section-preserving comparison](#/experiments/lp1-section-balance), [original baseline](#/experiments/lp1-word-length-balance), and [search-space explanation](#/wiki/search-space).\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp1-section-order/article.md",

    {
