    {
      "path": "experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/comparison.svg",
      "caption": "All 77 output byte streams are unchanged. The 41 abnormal exits become explicit iterator-guard rejections; this improves diagnostics without establishing absence of hidden data."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Original JPEGs: guarded OutGuess build comparison\n\n## What this test asks\n\nThe original default-key sweep had 41 abnormal exits. Those failures leave an important question: did the retrieval reach an identifiable error condition, and would a more explicit check change the extracted bytes?\n\nThis variant uses a clean build with three diagnostic guards. A guard checks a condition before an operation that would otherwise be invalid and stops with an explanatory message. Here the checks concern the retrieval bit position, iterator capacity, and a zero iterator value used by a remainder operation. They are diagnostic changes, not a new decryption method.\n\nThe [original baseline](#/experiments/outguess-default-key) remains available with its unchanged results. Both records belong to the same experiment family.\n\n## What stayed fixed\n\nThe inputs are all 75 manuscript JPEGs plus the 2014 opening image and compasses cover, in their original bytes. Image hashes, the literal key `Default key`, and the 20-second timeout match the baseline. No image was recompressed or edited. The ten known payload controls run first; a control failure would stop the sweep.\n\nThe scope and runner were committed as `40890c5` before execution. The earlier 13-case pilot helped establish the build procedure; those cases are included here and are not presented as unseen validation. This is one complete 77-image comparison, not a search over keys or build settings.\n\n## What changed\n\nThe recorded executable was compiled afresh from upstream commit `24810e14327c2bbeedeaadd3e24491f2a4425c02`, with the documented Windows portability changes and explicit guard patches. All 54 C files were compiled; object files from the original build were not reused. The build specification records compiler identity, source hashes and commands.\n\nThe clean executable differs in hash from the archived pilot executable, although it reproduced all 13 pilot results exactly. The full comparison below uses the clean executable. This does not establish bit-for-bit reproducible compilation across toolchains.\n\n## Results\n\n| Baseline outcome | Guarded outcome | Images |\n| --- | --- | ---: |\n| Successful exit | Same successful exit, diagnostic and bytes | 31 |\n| Existing rejection | Same rejection, diagnostic and bytes | 5 |\n| Abnormal exit | Explicit zero-iterator guard; unchanged empty output | 41 |\n\nAll ten positive controls match. The 31 successful exits consist of those ten controls and 21 unverified outputs. Every one of the 77 payload byte streams matches the baseline exactly; no new candidate output appeared.\n\nAll 41 changed cases report `Guard: iterator skipmod zero`, with their individual bit counts and offsets retained in the saved report. For example, LP1-14 reports `Guard: iterator skipmod zero at off=645437 bits=645682`. The guarded build checks this zero value before the iterator's remainder operation.\n\nThe [comparison graphic](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/comparison.svg) summarizes the counts. The [per-image comparison](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/comparison.json) and [complete diagnostics](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/report.json) retain the underlying evidence.\n\n## What the result means\n\nThe new build gives a specific diagnostic for all 41 previously abnormal cases. This is useful for investigating the implementation and for preventing those failures from being mistaken for clean negative results.\n\nIt does not authenticate the 21 candidate outputs. It does not prove any image lacks hidden data. Both executables share the same upstream source and Windows port, so this is not validation by an independent implementation or another platform. The guarded run is also not a captured stack trace from the original executable.\n\n## Reproduce the saved comparison\n\nDownload this experiment's bundle and the original-images archive, then extract both into the same folder, preserving their paths. Follow the bundle's START-HERE file to verify the archive and required image hashes. From that folder run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/compare.py --check\n```\n\nThis needs Python and the supplied data, but does not execute OutGuess. It verifies the plan dependencies and image hashes, checks both sets of saved outputs, and compares bytes and diagnostics directly. It recomputes the saved comparison instead of trusting its reported equality flags.\n\nTo regenerate the chart after that audit:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/figure.py\n```\n\n## Repeat retrieval from a source build\n\nSupply a clean checkout of the pinned upstream source and a compatible MinGW-W64 GCC toolchain. The included build script does not fetch or install these dependencies. Choose an output directory that does not yet exist:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/outguess-guard-pilot/build.py --source /path/to/outguess-source --output /path/to/new-build\npython experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/run.py --outguess /path/to/new-build/outguess.exe --output /path/to/new-results\n```\n\nThe runner requires the recorded executable hash. If compilation produces a different hash, preserve its build report and define a separate comparison; do not overwrite the expected hash to make the check pass. The new-results directory must not already exist. The saved-evidence audit above checks the committed results, not this new directory. To rerun retrieval and compare directly with the committed results, use `run.py --outguess /path/to/new-build/outguess.exe --check`.\n\n## Remaining work\n\nHuman review is pending. An independently documented platform or implementation would address a different uncertainty from the guard comparison. Candidate-payload analysis should be a separate bounded experiment, retaining all outputs and avoiding the assumption that process success implies a message.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "3bf3c1ee82423ab6565366c07d1bdfb147edd12b07268539da595d43736bfa1f",

  "article": "## What changed from the baseline\n\nThe [full-corpus comparison](#/experiments/parallel-languages) used 1,012 evaluation sentences per language. Here we divide that evaluation split into **eight consecutive, disjoint blocks** and compare shorter passages. Each block contains the same sentence IDs in all eight languages. No sentences were chosen because their statistics looked promising.\n\nThe first four blocks contain 127 sentences each, and the last four contain 126. Exact one-based sentence ranges are recorded in the results. The plan was committed before block scoring; its dependency hash was then refreshed for a chart-only change in the baseline, before scoring began. The tokenization and distance definitions are unchanged.\n\n## Results\n\n**English is the closest of the eight language profiles to the pooled manuscript in all eight blocks, in each of the three representations.** This supports the stability of that relative ranking across these shorter passages. It does not identify the plaintext language.\n\nUsing letter units, the block sizes and manuscript distances are:\n\n| Language | Tokens per block, range | Word-length distance, range |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| English | 2,613–3,002 | 0.0710–0.1035 |\n| Finnish | 1,927–2,105 | 0.3726–0.4316 |\n| French | 3,047–3,318 | 0.1731–0.2079 |\n| German | 2,623–2,927 | 0.1696–0.1961 |\n| Italian | 2,880–3,181 | 0.2274–0.2467 |\n| Portuguese | 2,818–3,147 | 0.2007–0.2300 |\n| Spanish | 3,106–3,467 | 0.2091–0.2402 |\n| Welsh | 2,884–3,206 | 0.1416–0.1940 |\n\nThe target has 2,896 rune tokens. These are smaller aligned passages, not exactly size-matched samples: their token counts range from **1,927 to 3,467**. Translating the same content changes word counts. Keeping the same sentence ranges preserves the content control; truncating every language at exactly 2,896 words would no longer compare exactly the same passages. This design documents that tradeoff rather than hiding it.\n\n## Does the statistic recognize known languages at this scale?\n\nFor each block, we compare its word-length histogram against all eight full development-language histograms. The closest development profile is the corresponding language in **64 of 64 decisions**, separately for letter units, accent-folded letters, and GP grouping. The raw report includes every distance and the full confusion matrices, including zeros.\n\nThat is a control on these eight translated languages within FLORES. It is not a success rate for cipher language identification. The corpus shares translation practices and source genre; the manuscript does not. The three representations also reuse the same text and are not independent replications.\n\n## Bounds and limitations\n\n- All 1,012 evaluation sentences are used once per language, with no overlap between blocks. Development text is used only for the reference profiles.\n- A source article can cross a block boundary. Blocks are therefore not independent draws, and the 64 decisions are not treated as independent trials. No binomial accuracy interval or language posterior is calculated.\n- The manuscript remains pooled LP2-00–55, with headings and the baseline boundary convention. This does not test each section separately.\n- Word-length comparison requires preserved boundaries and one ciphertext rune per counted plaintext unit. GP grouping remains an orthographic sensitivity, not a validated phonetic transcription.\n- No genre-matched corpus or known decoded LP control is included in this variant. The separate [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) now covers the nine documented LP sections. A genre-matched corpus remains open.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nThe experiment download includes the aligned corpus, token ledger, baseline helper, independent tokenizer, frozen plan and result ledger. Python 3 standard library only; no network, API or model is used.\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command verifies input hashes and recomputes the full report. The second independently reconstructs all 192 block profiles with a regex tokenizer and exact rational total-variation distances, checks all nearest-reference decisions, and verifies that the block ranges cover the evaluation sentences exactly once. Human review is pending.\n\n[Results and confusion matrices](experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/results.json) · [Frozen plan](experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/plan.json) · [Baseline distributions and source attribution](#/experiments/parallel-languages)\n\nFLORES source text and this derived account are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0. See the source attribution included with the baseline files.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "db2005dd2fbebe5e0afe202cc5a7aecc4ca60f9ae8a3b059b6deb028220183d5",

    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }

    {

  "article": "## What this comparison tells us\n\n**English is closest by word lengths among these eight languages.** The ordering of other close candidates changes when a fixed GP-style grouping is applied to all eight. This is a comparison of statistical shapes under stated assumptions. It does not identify the plaintext or decipher a word.\n\nThe experiment uses translations of the **same 997 development sentences and 1,012 evaluation sentences** from FLORES-200. The languages were fixed before scoring: English, Welsh, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Finnish. They give a manageable Latin-script comparison without adding a transliteration model for other scripts. They are not a shortlist inferred from the manuscript, and the ranking is not a search across all languages.\n\nThe plan and source files were committed in `738a812` before any scores were calculated. It is a predeclared comparison within this project, not an external preregistration. Human review is pending.\n\n## Word-length results\n\nThe distance is **total variation** between word-length distributions: half the sum of their absolute frequency differences. Zero means identical distributions; one means no overlap. We count lengths 1 through 15 separately and put longer words in a final 16+ bin. A value of 0.084 is a distance, not an 8.4% chance of anything.\n\n| Language | Letters | GP grouping sensitivity |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| English | 0.0840 | 0.1148 |\n| Welsh | 0.1721 | 0.1731 |\n| German | 0.1757 | 0.1708 |\n| French | 0.1827 | 0.1759 |\n| Portuguese | 0.2131 | 0.2058 |\n| Spanish | 0.2240 | 0.2127 |\n| Italian | 0.2359 | 0.2311 |\n| Finnish | 0.4022 | 0.3927 |\n\n[Open the comparison chart](experiments/records/parallel-languages/comparison.svg). The chart shows the same results with article-resampling ranges. The JSON also contains the accent-folded letter comparison, which keeps the same language order.\n\nThe ordering depends on the counting convention. A language ranking is conditional on both the corpus and the assumed relationship between plaintext units and ciphertext runes. The full table keeps every tested candidate visible.\n\n## Why the rankings differ\n\nThe manuscript has a pronounced peak at length three: **24.86% of its tokens contain three runes**. The language profiles differ in how much mass they place at each length. The distribution chart shows the manuscript first, followed by all eight languages alphabetically, using identical scales and the same styling for every language.\n\nThe first-place result still has a visible mismatch: English has 19.07% three-letter words, below the manuscript's three-rune share. A ranking measures relative closeness among the tested profiles; it does not establish that the nearest profile is a good explanation of the ciphertext.\n\n[Open all nine distribution panels](experiments/records/parallel-languages/distributions.svg). Lengths 9 and above are combined only for display; scoring retains the original 16 bins. Every full distribution is also available in the results JSON.\n\n## The assumptions that make lengths useful\n\nThis comparison requires manuscript word boundaries to preserve plaintext word boundaries, and one counted plaintext unit to correspond to one ciphertext rune. A position-dependent substitution can preserve lengths even when letter frequencies change. Inserted nulls, deleted symbols, word splitting, different spacing, or units representing syllables can break the comparison.\n\nThe manuscript target is the existing [rune-token ledger](exports/unsolved-word-tokens.json): **2,896 tokens and 12,956 runes from LP2-00–55**, including headings. Line wraps and slash wraps are removed; tokens can continue across page boundaries. Internal apostrophes count zero, and decimal labels are excluded. See [word lengths](#/wiki/word-lengths) for the exact boundary convention and its historical alternatives. Pooling the pages assumes their aggregate is meaningful; it does not establish that every section has one language or cipher.\n\nFor FLORES, letters are lowercased and normalized to NFC. Alphabetic runs are words; internal straight or curly apostrophes are removed without splitting the word. Hyphens and other nonletters separate words. Numbers contribute no letters. Each sentence is tokenized independently. This is an explicit mechanical convention, not a linguist's definition of a word. The comparison retains every aligned sentence; it does not truncate each language to a different passage to equalize word totals.\n\nThe GP sensitivity folds combining accents and greedily groups ING, TH, EO, NG, OE, AE, IA, IO and EA, longest first. ING/NG, IO/IA, K/C and Z/S share symbols. Other letters remain. **This is not a validated translation into Gematria Primus.** Pronunciation, ambiguous segmentation and unsupported letters remain unresolved. A supplementary mechanical Welsh-digraph calculation is retained in the raw data as a representation check, not as a separate candidate category or a preferred model. It groups CH, DD, FF, NG, LL, PH, RH and TH and gives a length distance of 0.1466; it does not resolve morphological parsing. The raw-letter and GP profiles can contain more than 29 distinct symbols, so they cannot be literal bijective mappings into a 29-rune alphabet as written. This inventory mismatch is reported in the downloadable results rather than silently repaired by deleting rare letters.\n\n## Repetition gives a different test\n\nIoC is the probability that two different sampled positions contain the same symbol. Adjacent repetition here counts equal neighbors **within words only**. Both require stronger assumptions than lengths: equality must survive a fixed one-to-one substitution. They are not preserved by a general polyalphabetic cipher.\n\n| Text, using letter units | IoC | Equal adjacent pairs |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| Unsolved rune target | 0.03448 | 0.63% |\n| English | 0.06597 | 2.42% |\n| Welsh | 0.06387 | 5.74% |\n| German | 0.07344 | 2.33% |\n| French | 0.06912 | 2.42% |\n| Portuguese | 0.07072 | 1.00% |\n| Spanish | 0.07111 | 0.77% |\n| Italian | 0.07305 | 4.57% |\n| Finnish | 0.07282 | 9.31% |\n\nThe language profiles have letter IoCs between **0.06387 and 0.07344**, far from the target's **0.03448**. None of these profiles supplies a close single-substitution explanation of the pooled manuscript. The GP sensitivity does not remove that discrepancy. Spanish is closest on the adjacent-repeat measure, yet has a much poorer word-length match. These conflicting rankings are why we do not blend the measures into an unexplained “language likelihood.”\n\nThis does not eliminate Welsh, English or any other language under a different cipher. It weakens the proposed fixed-substitution comparison under these text and unit conventions. See [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) for what different transformations preserve.\n\n## Controls and sampling sensitivity\n\nEach development-language word-length profile was compared with each evaluation-language profile. The nearest development profile identified the corresponding evaluation language **8 out of 8 times in each of the three representations**. That is a useful check that this dataset and statistic can distinguish the chosen languages at this sample size. It is not 100% accuracy on unknown manuscripts: there are only eight whole-document controls, drawn from the same benchmark, and they are much longer than the target.\n\nFor the error bars we resample the **281 source-article URL groups** in the evaluation split, with replacement, 200 times using seed 3301. All sentences from a sampled article are kept. The same article draw is used for all eight languages, preserving the matched-content comparison and avoiding treating every sentence as independent. English has the smallest length distance in all 200 draws in all three representations. This is stability to this corpus resampling—not a 100% probability that the manuscript is English. The target transcription is held fixed; these intervals omit uncertainty about its boundaries, genre and cipher.\n\nFLORES contains translated web material. It controls subject matter across languages, but not the difference between that material and Liber Primus's philosophical style, historical spelling or possible nonstandard prose. Translation practices can also affect lengths. A separately fixed, genre-matched parallel corpus remains a follow-up. The [exact-token control](#/experiments/target-sized-languages) now checks complete 2,896-token samples: all reference samples identify their own language profile, but every manuscript-to-profile distance exceeds the corresponding observed control range. Those ranges are descriptive, not confidence limits or rejection thresholds. The [known-LP reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) is now complete as a computational comparison, with human review pending. A separate [shorter aligned-block variant](#/experiments/parallel-language-blocks) now checks eight disjoint evaluation blocks per language; it preserves matching sentences rather than enforcing exactly equal word counts.\n\n## Reproduce it\n\nDownload this experiment's bundle. It includes the source translations, source-article metadata, plan, token ledger, scripts, result JSON and chart. No API, account, model download or network request is needed to rerun the analysis; Python 3's standard library is enough.\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/parallel-languages/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/parallel-languages/check.py\npython experiments/records/parallel-languages/distribution_figure.py --check\n```\n\nThe first command verifies input hashes, recomputes the comparisons and the 200 resamples, and checks the saved report and chart. Without `--check`, it writes those two outputs. The second uses a separate regex tokenizer and integer-count formulas to verify the 24 language profiles, additional digraph sensitivity, manuscript profile, IoC, repeated neighbors, distances and ordering. It does not independently reimplement the bootstrap. The final command checks that the distribution chart matches the saved counts; it does not perform another experiment. The ledger itself has a separate [transcription/word-length reproduction](#/wiki/word-lengths).\n\n[Raw results](experiments/records/parallel-languages/results.json) · [Frozen plan](experiments/records/parallel-languages/plan.json) · [Source attribution](experiments/records/parallel-languages/SOURCE.txt)\n\n## Sources and reuse\n\n- [FLORES-200 documentation](https://github.com/facebookresearch/flores/blob/main/flores200/README.md): aligned translation benchmark and language list.\n- [Original archive](https://dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/nllb/flores200_dataset.tar.gz): exact extracted translation and metadata files; archive and extracted-file hashes are recorded in the plan.\n- [Dataset card and license](https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/flores): Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International. Source translations are redistributed unchanged. This derived analysis and its article are also offered under CC BY-SA 4.0.\n\n## Check against known LP readings\n\nThe [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) now tests all nine established reading sections and their pool. The pool ranks closest to English, while some individual sections do not. It also documents how LP2-56's embedded hash distorts an unfiltered letter-token count. This supplies a manuscript-specific caution beyond the within-FLORES controls.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/parallel-languages/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "2770ff9ecd31f24a8f66a76b1da18e0ca7f518962f4bde8b15dceb001bddaa4c",

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "exports/figures/position-divisor-bound.svg",
      "caption": "LP2-00: the same F rune occurs at positions 7, 17 and 58. Subtraction removes the unknown origin. The stride assumption determines the conclusion."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Can each rune label a divisor of its position?\n\n**Not with consecutive positions, under the rule tested here.** Every nonempty rune page in LP2-00–55 contains repeated occurrences whose spacing makes a fixed divisor greater than one impossible, regardless of where counting starts. This is a fresh reproduction of the supplied closure archive's C11 claim, not an original discovery.\n\n## Define the rule before testing it\n\nLet i be a zero-based rune position within a page. Choose an integer origin N and a fixed stride s. Assign each rune r an integer divisor q[r] greater than one, then require:\n\n```text\nq[r] divides N + s*i whenever position i contains r\n```\n\nThe same rune must keep the same divisor throughout that page. Divisors need not be prime, distinct, or equal to Gematria Primus values. Allowing all integers greater than one makes this test more permissive than an assignment restricted to primes. Each page may use its own origin, stride and assignment.\n\nThis is a necessary condition for a direct smallest-factor or largest-factor labeling proposal. It does not test prime-derived keys combined with plaintext or an arbitrary operation that merely uses prime numbers.\n\n## Why the origin cancels\n\nIf q divides both N+s*i and N+s*j, it divides their difference s*(j−i). The unknown N disappears. For several occurrences, q must therefore divide the stride multiplied by the gcd of the position gaps.\n\nFor unit stride, a gap gcd of 1 would require q to divide 1. That contradicts q > 1. Running the page backwards changes the origin and stride sign, not this obstruction.\n\nA rune appearing only once has no gap constraint. Two occurrences with gap 1 already suffice; otherwise several gaps may be needed. The report records every occurrence and, where available, a three-occurrence gcd-one witness. It uses gcd 0 for an empty set of gaps; that means no restriction from this particular test, not impossibility.\n\n## A witness on LP2-00\n\nF occurs at zero-based rune positions **7, 17 and 58**. Thus a fixed divisor must divide both 10 and 51 under unit stride. Their gcd is 1. This single repeated rune already rules out the model on that page; the report records the other rune labels as well.\n\nThese are positions in the filtered rune stream, including the heading. They are not image coordinates, Latin-letter offsets or positions that count punctuation.\n\n## What the full retest covers\n\nThe program reads all 56 archived text files LP2-00–55, retains alphabet runes and headings, and starts each page independently. All **55 nonempty streams** have at least one gcd-one rune. LP2-50 has no alphabet runes in this transcription and is skipped; its alphanumeric grid is not converted into runes.\n\nEvery page therefore excludes both forward and reverse unit-stride constructions, even when the origin and arbitrary integer divisor labels are chosen independently for that page. This is an exact contradiction under the stated model, not a low probability or a finite search over origins.\n\n## Why arbitrary strides remain different\n\nWith a gcd-one witness, the general condition is **q divides s**. It excludes a stride coprime to that rune's divisor. It does not exclude every nonunit stride.\n\nFor a concrete counterexample, set N=2, s=2 and q[r]=2 for every rune. Every position N+s*i is even, so every recorded rune passes the divisibility condition on every page. This construction assigns the same divisor to different runes, which the tested necessary condition permits. It supplies no decoding rule and does not identify which rune to emit at a position.\n\nIf a proposal requires distinct labels, literal GP primes, or a deterministic factor-selection rule, those extra requirements need separate analysis. The counterexample refutes the broader claim that this divisibility condition alone excludes all strides; it is not a successful cipher.\n\n## Reproduce and independently check\n\nDownload the experiment ZIP and keep its folders intact. Python 3's standard library is sufficient; no network, AI calls or additional packages are needed.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/position-divisor-labels/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/position-divisor-labels/check.py\n```\n\nThe first program uses distances from each rune's first occurrence. The independent checker reads page JSON and computes the gcd of all pairwise occurrence distances. It also verifies every displayed triple, the stride-two counterexample on all 55 pages, a valid unit-stride control, and 450 small synthetic origin/stride cases.\n\nBoth text sources share archival ancestry: agreement is a computation check, not an independent manuscript transcription review. The earlier archive cites a Lean proof; this package provides elementary reasoning and fresh integer checks, without claiming that the Lean development was rerun.\n\n## Limits and reopening conditions\n\nChanging which characters advance the clock, resetting within a page, changing a rune's divisor over time, selecting an irregular sequence of integers, or transforming the factor labels changes the model. Such proposals are not ruled out here. A transcription correction also requires a new run. This result belongs alongside other bounded exclusions, not under a heading claiming that prime-based ciphers are impossible.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/position-divisor-labels/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "2ca802f7f836a90709cb254ff52e5590a11c2b797b7ffe677920a38f2c9c6689",

    "id": "measurement",
    "label": "Manuscript measurement",
    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }
}

  "article": "## Why test a whole search?\n\nA candidate can look better simply because we tried more keys. Comparing that winner with one randomly chosen wrong key ignores the selection that produced it. This experiment repeats an entire declared search on null ciphertexts, retaining its best score each time.\n\nThe best null scores rise as the nested dictionary grows from one to 256 keys, but none crosses the fixed −5.5 acceptance threshold in this grid. Searches of positive ciphertext also fail that threshold when the true key is absent. Appending the true key makes every positive control recover exactly and pass. These outcomes describe this finite search; they are not a guarantee against false positives in larger or different searches.\n\n## Three conditions, kept separate\n\n| Condition | Ciphertext | Keys searched | What it checks |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| Null | Reproducible uniform pseudorandom rune indices | A declared wrong-key dictionary | The best score selected from the whole dictionary under this null generator. |\n| Positive, key absent | A known rune prefix encrypted by addition modulo 29 | The same dictionary, excluding its true seed | What a search reports when its intended answer is outside its bounds. |\n| Positive, key included | The same positive ciphertext | That dictionary plus its true key | Whether inclusion recovers the known answer and whether it wins the scoring comparison. |\n\nThe included condition has **one more candidate** than the stated wrong-key budget. At budget 256 it compares 257 candidates. Its known key is not secretly inserted into the other conditions, and its exact-recovery check is separate from score acceptance.\n\n## Inputs and bounds\n\nAll nine known-reading traces contribute their first 240 output rune indices, or their full length when shorter. Their lengths range from 85 to 240 runes. These are existing trace outputs, not edited English converted back into runes. No section is removed because of a poor score or unusual content.\n\nFor each section, 32 replicates generate a null ciphertext and a positive ciphertext of that section's length. Each null uses a fresh, recorded Python pseudorandom-generator seed and uniform draws from indices 0–28. Each positive uses the known prefix and a recorded derived key. The paired controls share length and search settings; they do not share ciphertext.\n\nThe candidate keys use SHA-256 over a fixed ASCII seed label and a four-byte big-endian counter, with digest bytes reduced modulo 29. Because 256 is not divisible by 29, this reduction is biased. It is an explicit fixture, not a uniform-pad claim. Candidate seeds are 0–255; positive seeds are 100000–100031 and therefore absent from that dictionary.\n\nFor every candidate, subtract its key from the ciphertext modulo 29, transliterate with the canonical rune labels, and average the English quadgram log scores. The unseen-quadgram count is 0.01 and the threshold is −5.5, inherited unchanged from the [scorer controls](#/experiments/english-scorer-controls). There are no offsets, alternate signs, skip rules or word-boundary adjustments.\n\n## Nested search budgets\n\nEvery search retains all 256 individual candidate scores and examines dictionary prefixes of 1, 4, 16, 64 and 256 keys. A larger budget contains every candidate in the smaller one. Its maximum therefore cannot decrease. Ties use the smallest seed ID, including when comparing an appended true key.\n\nThe figures preserve all nine source sections. At each budget, a dot is the median of the 32 best scores and the vertical line is their full observed range. Neither is a confidence interval. All panels share a score scale. The positive included condition has a constant score within a section because exact decryption returns the same known rune prefix despite different encryption keys.\n\n| Wrong-key budget | Null accepted | Positive accepted, true key absent | Positive exact and accepted, true key included |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| 1 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (2 candidates) |\n| 4 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (5 candidates) |\n| 16 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (17 candidates) |\n| 64 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (65 candidates) |\n| 256 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (257 candidates) |\n\nThese are counts over the fixed grid, not independent-trial accuracy estimates. The full CSV keeps each section separate across all 135 section/budget/condition combinations. The JSON retains all 147,456 wrong-key scores, 288 true-key controls, ciphertexts, seeds, candidate hashes and search winners.\n\n## What a zero count means\n\nWe observed no threshold exceedances among these null searches. That does not prove the threshold is safe for a million-key search, a beam decoder, several language models, or repeated human choices about which output to keep. Such procedures offer different opportunities to find a high-scoring candidate and need their own controls.\n\nThe sections share source material, the dictionary is reused, and budgets are nested. Repetition does not turn this into 288 independent texts drawn from all possible plaintext. The null generator is also a chosen model, not an established description of the manuscript. We do not estimate a probability that a manuscript candidate is correct, pool the scores into an anomaly verdict, or infer a cipher family.\n\nThe [decoder alignment controls](#/experiments/decoder-skip-controls) demonstrate a complementary limitation: even a correct key can fail under an unsuitable decoder, and an incorrect rune sequence can pass a language score. Here the positive controls validate only ordinary modular addition and this declared dictionary search.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP with its folder structure intact. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient; there are no network requests, API calls or paid services.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/search-maximum-controls/run.py --check\npython scripts/check_search_maximum_controls.py experiments/records/search-maximum-controls/results.json --receipt my-search-audit.json\npython experiments/records/search-maximum-controls/plot.py\n```\n\nThe independent checker imports no producer functions. It rebuilds the source prefixes, null ciphertexts and derived keys, checks every candidate hash, recalculates scores using counted quadgrams, and reconstructs every winner and tie decision. It also checks monotonic maxima and the additional candidate count when the true key is appended. All 288 paired searches passed; human review remains pending.\n\nThe practical lesson is to compare a selected result with controls that undergo the same selection. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [null models](#/wiki/null-models). A different dictionary, decoder, scoring rule or adaptive workflow should be a documented variant, with the complete search repeated in its controls.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/search-maximum-controls/article.md",

    "description": "Checks a search, decoder or scorer using synthetic inputs or reference text; it does not identify the cipher of an unsolved page."
  }
}

  "sources": [
    {
      "label": "Pinned repository discussion motivating short-seed controls",
      "url": "https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/PAPER.md"
    }
  ],
  "related": [
    "search-maximum-controls",
    "decoder-skip-controls"
  ],
  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/seed-crib-controls/prefix-matches.svg",
      "caption": "Minimum and maximum surviving seed counts across every search in each group. Counts are dependent control results, not confidence intervals. All five crib lengths and zero-result conditions are retained."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Does matching the opening text identify a seed?\n\nA short readable opening can have several explanations. This experiment plants a known 95-rune passage under two fixed keystream generators, searches a finite seed dictionary, and asks whether seeds that reproduce the opening also predict the remaining text. No candidate is selected by looking at that remaining text.\n\nA **crib** is an assumed exact plaintext sequence at an exact position. Here the crib is supplied as part of the control. It is not guessed from the ciphertext or inferred from a language score. The **withheld suffix** is everything after the crib: the part reserved for checking a prediction.\n\nWith two crib runes, every tested search retains several seeds. Only the true generating pairs recover the complete passage. At four or more crib runes, those generating pairs are the only survivors in the searches that include them; the other controls retain none. This is a result for these fixtures and dictionaries, not a general four-rune requirement.\n\n## What is searched?\n\nThe plaintext is the 95 output rune indices from the known reading of LP2-57. New ciphertexts are generated from it. This is not a new attempt to decrypt the original LP2-57 image, and it supplies no claim about the unsolved pages.\n\nThe two generators use SHA-256 and SHA-512. Each hashes the ASCII domain separator `liberpedia-seed-control:v1:`, followed by a four-byte unsigned big-endian seed and a four-byte unsigned big-endian counter starting at zero. Digest bytes of 232 or greater are discarded; the remaining bytes are reduced modulo 29. Digests are concatenated until 95 indices are available. There are no skips, offsets, resets or alternate signs.\n\nEach generator plants seeds 17, 4095 and 4096. Each search tests seeds **0 through 4095**, inclusive, under one generator. Seed 4096 is deliberately absent from both search dictionaries even though it is a valid generator input. Thus an unsuccessful search can simply mean the needed seed is outside its bounds.\n\nEncryption is `cipher[i] = (plain[i] + key[i]) mod 29`. A seed survives when it reproduces every assumed crib rune at the start. Every survivor is retained; there is no English score, best-candidate ranking or phrase selection. Its complete decoded sequence is then compared with the known plaintext, keeping full-passage equality and withheld-suffix equality separate.\n\n## Results\n\nThe figure reports the range of candidate counts across the searches in each control group. These ranges are not confidence intervals. The incorrect-crib group changes only the first rune by adding one modulo 29, leaving the rest of the assumed opening unchanged. It includes both matching and mismatched search generators.\n\n| Control | Searches per crib length | Survivors with 2 crib runes | Survivors with 4, 8, 16 or 32 crib runes |\n| --- | ---: | --- | --- |\n| Correct crib; generating pair included | 4 | 4, 6, 11, 8 | Exactly 1 per search |\n| Correct crib; matching generator but seed outside range | 2 | 5, 4 | 0 |\n| Correct crib; wrong generator | 6 | 8, 5, 10, 6, 8, 2 | 0 |\n| Incorrect first crib rune | 12 | 6, 5, 2, 7, 4, 3, 8, 6, 7, 4, 4, 6 | 0 |\n\nAt length two, the four included-pair searches contain 29 survivors in total. Four are the true generating pairs; the other 25 fail to predict the complete 93-rune withheld suffix. All survivors in the other three control groups also fail that complete suffix test. They may agree with individual withheld runes, which is why the full report preserves both exact equality and the number of correct positions.\n\nFor all longer tested cribs, each included-pair search retains exactly the true seed, which recovers all 95 runes. An incorrect first crib rune prevents full-passage equality by construction; the independently evaluated suffix test is a separate check.\n\nThe complete summary retains all **120 cells**, including zero-survivor cases. The full JSON also stores every searched keystream, every planted ciphertext and every surviving candidate's decoded sequence. A generating-pair identity and an exact finite-stream match are conceptually different; no alternative pair recovers the whole passage in these controls.\n\n## What an empty search establishes\n\nAn empty result excludes only the tested generator/seed pairs under the exact crib and alignment. It does not exclude seeds outside the dictionary, other generators, another seed encoding, a different crib, an unknown offset or a different cipher mechanism. The two omitted-seed fixtures demonstrate this directly: their ciphertexts are generated by a tested generator, yet the bounded correct-crib searches retain no seed once the crib reaches four runes.\n\nThese cells reuse one plaintext and fixed dictionaries. They are dependent controls, not independent samples from a population of ciphers. Short prefixes can match accidentally; no probability that an LP proposal is correct follows from these counts. Random-looking ciphertext also does not establish an independent one-time pad.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nExtract this experiment's ZIP with folders intact, or use the repository. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient; no additional corpus, original-image download, API or model is needed.\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/seed-crib-controls/run.py --check\n```\n\nThe command reconstructs the result, independently checks every stream and survivor, and compares the complete summary and figure. Use `--output seed-replay` instead to retain newly generated reports in a new directory. The plot can also be regenerated with `python experiments/records/seed-crib-controls/plot.py`.\n\nThe protocol was committed before candidate generation. The checker imports no producer code: it separately packs seed/counter bytes, uses division to implement rejection conversion and checks compatibility by directly encrypting the assumed crib. Both implementations share Python's hash primitives. Boundary and exhaustive toy controls test byte order, the 231/232 cutoff and the difference between prefix, suffix and whole-text agreement. Human review remains pending.\n\n## Related explanations\n\nRead [search spaces and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for interpreting an empty search, [one-time pads and short seeds](#/wiki/one-time-pad) for the identification limits, and [search-maximum controls](#/experiments/search-maximum-controls) for the different problem of selecting the highest language score.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/seed-crib-controls/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "cc328de8bb18f1b8d7f3d9178391996dd3cf6577898dc92babc12183d433b8da",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "control",
    "label": "Control",
    "description": "Checks a search, decoder or scorer using synthetic inputs or reference text; it does not identify the cipher of an unsolved page."
  }
}

  "article": "# Selected phrase and MYRMELEONTIDAE word sums\n\nThis variant changes the baseline's candidate list to five supplied words: PROVE, WORTHIER, FIND, TRUTHS and MYRMELEONTIDAE. The first four were proposed against totals 131, 151, 151 and 131; the last against 809. It checks those selected matches without claiming that the resulting phrase or name is recovered plaintext.\n\n## What changes from the baseline?\n\nThe [baseline word-sum audit](#/experiments/mixed-square-word-sums) tests sixteen other supplied word-and-total pairs, including FIND. This variant retains the same 29-label alphabet, V-to-U normalization, exhaustive segmentation procedure and prime-value summation. Only the candidate list and proposed targets change. FIND is intentionally retained as a shared check.\n\nThe candidate list was fixed before enumeration, but the supplied words were already selected for their claimed numerical matches. This is an exploratory audit, not an unbiased measure of how frequently words match these targets.\n\n## All ten segmentations\n\nEvery segmentation is retained below. A slash separates rune labels; adjacent Latin letters inside one label belong to a single rune.\n\n| Candidate | Rune labels | Sum | Proposed target matched? |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| PROVE | P / R / O / U / E | 131 | Yes |\n| WORTHIER | W / O / R / TH / I / E / R | 151 | Yes |\n| WORTHIER | W / O / R / T / H / I / E / R | 228 | No |\n| FIND | F / I / N / D | 151 | Yes |\n| TRUTHS | T / R / U / TH / S | 131 | Yes |\n| TRUTHS | T / R / U / T / H / S | 208 | No |\n| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / EO / N / T / I / D / A / E | 809 | Yes |\n| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / EO / N / T / I / D / AE | 746 | No |\n| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / E / O / N / T / I / D / A / E | 842 | No |\n| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / E / O / N / T / I / D / AE | 779 | No |\n\nAll five targets are achievable, each by one segmentation. PROVE and FIND each have only one segmentation under the declared rules. WORTHIER and TRUTHS each have two; MYRMELEONTIDAE has four.\n\n## The 809 match requires a particular segmentation\n\nMYRMELEONTIDAE gives 809 when EO is combined but the final A and E are separate. Combining both EO and AE gives 746. Separating both pairs gives 842; combining only the final AE gives 779. These alternatives differ because a two-letter rune's prime value is not the sum of its two separate letters' values.\n\nA converter that always consumes the longest available label would choose EO and AE and return 746. A converter that always treats each Latin letter separately would return 842. The proposed 809 result is therefore possible within the exhaustive search, but it is not determined by the spelling alone. No evidence here selects that segmentation as the manuscript's intended representation.\n\n## What the phrase match establishes\n\nThe matching totals for PROVE WORTHIER FIND TRUTHS are 131, 151, 151 and 131. That verifies four arithmetic assignments. It does not recover their order, grammar or intended meaning from the square. Choosing words for their fitting totals and then observing that those totals are prime is not a second independent test: the target numbers already supplied that property.\n\nThe [mixed-square guide](#/wiki/magic-squares) distinguishes LP1-05's 1033 square, LP1-16's 3301 square and the separate LP2-15 panel. This variant associates the first four targets with LP1-05 and 809 with LP1-16; it does not move the red 3299 from LP2-15 into either square. A claimed thematic relation of a word to insect imagery would require separate evidence and is not tested here.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/selected-phrase-word-sums/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/selected-phrase-word-sums/check.py\n```\n\nThe runner is byte-identical to the baseline runner and reads this variant's plan. Without `--check`, it prints the complete JSON report. The independent checker enumerates every cut/no-cut choice between Latin letters, rejects pieces absent from the alphabet, and verifies all retained segmentations and totals. Both commands passed in the extracted reproduction bundle. Python's standard library is sufficient; no dictionary download or hosted AI is involved.\n\n## Limits and next variants\n\nNo alternative words, synonyms or dictionary entries were searched. No cipher was applied to the manuscript, and no null model estimates the surprise of the selected words. The finding neither proves an intended phrase nor shows that these are the only fitting words.\n\nA broader word search must pin its vocabulary, normalization and segmentation policy, then retain all matches. A fixed longest-label policy would be a different variant. A cipher test using these candidates must specify the target pages, transform, key advancement and success criterion. The [rune-length bounds](#/wiki/prime-sums?section=length-bounds) can rule out impossible lengths before a dictionary search starts.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/selected-phrase-word-sums/article.md",

      "path": "experiments/records/target-sized-languages/comparison.svg",
      "caption": "Identical axes and styling for all eight languages. Blue ranges are observed reference-sample distances; diamonds are manuscript distances. Ranges are not confidence limits."

  "article": "## Why match the number of tokens?\n\nThe [aligned-language baseline](#/experiments/parallel-languages) compares the manuscript with much longer reference texts. This control asks a narrower question: how do those reference languages behave when each sample contains exactly **2,896 tokens**, the size of the unsolved rune-token target?\n\nEvery complete reference sample is nearest to its own language profile. However, **the manuscript is farther from every language profile than any of that language's reference samples are**. English is still the nearest of the eight candidates, but nearest does not mean that its profile closely explains the manuscript. These are observed distances, not probabilities or statistical rejection thresholds.\n\n## What is held fixed\n\nThe languages, translations, development profiles, three common representations and total-variation distance are inherited from the baseline. There is no fitted classifier or new language selection. Each evaluation translation is tokenized sentence by sentence, then divided in original order into disjoint blocks of 2,896 tokens. Every complete block is retained; the final incomplete remainder is counted and reported but not scored as an equal-size sample.\n\nThis produces seven blocks each for English and German, eight each for French, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish and Welsh, and five for Finnish. The three representations reuse the same texts. The resulting 177 profile checks are **not 177 independent trials**, and they are not pooled into a claimed general classification accuracy.\n\nEqual token counts do not preserve identical translated passages: different languages use different numbers of words for the same content. This control addresses size. The [aligned-block variant](#/experiments/parallel-language-blocks) separately preserves sentence ranges across languages. Neither controls for the difference between translated web material and Liber Primus's style.\n\n## Reading the distances\n\nEach sample is compared with all eight full development profiles using length bins 1 through 15 and 16+. Total variation is half the sum of the absolute differences in bin proportions. Zero means matching distributions; larger values mean greater separation. All distances are stored as exact rational numbers, and ties would be retained rather than broken by language order.\n\n| Language | Complete blocks per representation | Largest letter-control distance | Manuscript to letter profile |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| English | 7 | 0.0508 | 0.0831 |\n| Finnish | 5 | 0.0466 | 0.4051 |\n| French | 8 | 0.0514 | 0.1781 |\n| German | 7 | 0.0561 | 0.1665 |\n| Italian | 8 | 0.0436 | 0.2375 |\n| Portuguese | 8 | 0.0426 | 0.2114 |\n| Spanish | 8 | 0.0456 | 0.2230 |\n| Welsh | 8 | 0.0404 | 0.1650 |\n\n“Largest control distance” means the farthest observed sample from its own language's development profile. It is not a confidence limit. The manuscript lies beyond those observed ranges for all eight languages in all three representations, including GP-style grouping. That grouping is an orthographic sensitivity, not a validated conversion of each language into runes.\n\nWithin this corpus, all complete samples have a unique nearest profile matching their known language. The manuscript's nearest profile is English in all three representations. The report preserves every competing distance and the margin over the nearest competing language, so this statement can be checked without relying on a winner-only table.\n\n## A Unicode exception found before scoring\n\nThe original follow-up plan assumed that all three representations would preserve token boundaries. The implementation stopped when that check failed. Lowercasing the capital dotted I in “İzmir” creates an i followed by a combining dot; the inherited raw-letter tokenizer treats the mark as a separator. Accent folding removes it, joining the word. Three source sentences are affected.\n\nAn amendment was committed after inspecting that tokenization issue and before inspecting follow-up scores. The baseline tokenizer was not silently changed. Each representation is partitioned independently, its endpoint ledger is retained, and the report states whether boundaries agree. Folded letters and GP grouping do share boundaries. The original plan remains available alongside the amendment.\n\n## What this does not establish\n\nThe control does not identify the manuscript's language, eliminate the eight languages, or estimate a posterior probability. The sample ranges are small, adjacent blocks can share a source article, and both reference splits come from the same benchmark. The manuscript has different genre, spelling, unit and boundary uncertainties. Even its closest reference profile can therefore be a poor match for reasons other than language.\n\nThe [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) supplies a complementary warning: some short, established English sections rank nearest to other language profiles. The [cipher-invariants guide](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) explains which transformations preserve lengths and which change the assumptions behind this comparison.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nPython 3's standard library is sufficient; no API or model is involved. From the repository or extracted reproduction bundle, choose new output filenames:\n\n```sh\npython scripts/run_target_sized_languages.py --output my-language-controls.json\npython scripts/check_target_sized_languages.py my-language-controls.json --receipt my-language-audit.json\npython -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_target_sized_languages.py\n```\n\nThe independent checker imports neither the producer nor the baseline tokenizer. It reconstructs words with a regex tokenizer, calculates distances from integer histogram counts, and checks all sample boundaries, remainders, 177 profiles, competing distances, margins and summary decisions. Its saved receipt records the report and checker hashes. Computational verification has passed; human review remains pending.\n\nFLORES translations and this derived account are provided under CC BY-SA 4.0. The baseline's source attribution is included with the reproduction files.\n",

  "article": "## What was tested\n\nThe proposed 27 × 27 reading can be reproduced **when its selected cells and key nodes are supplied**. This experiment checks that arithmetic, the map itself, and the additional rules for predicting properties of the next block. It does not find the route from the manuscript without those selections.\n\nThe source is pinned to commit `d5eed3f10428372c7202ceebc65cc3bdead0819d`. Later edits to that repository are outside this result. The downloadable input records the coordinates, keys, source-file hashes and proposed output rune indices. No language model or language scorer chooses words in this replay.\n\n## Results at a glance\n\n| Check | Result | What it establishes |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Map compared with archived LP2-00–02 | 729 of 729 cells agree | The selected matrix uses our transcription in page order |\n| Main reading | 17 blocks, 61 rune subtractions reproduce | Correct arithmetic for supplied choices |\n| Alternative SOON block | 4 further subtractions reproduce | A second supplied route produces the same word |\n| Next-key signature | 16 of 16 transitions match | Fit to the recorded route |\n| Next axis and boundary role | Each matches 16 of 16 | Further fit to the same route, not independent discoveries |\n| Ciphertext coverage | 54 distinct cells of 729, about 7.4% | The proposed reading is a selection, with reused cells |\n| Same SOON key from three nodes | Horizontal / diagonal / diagonal | Key equality does not settle the node choice |\n\n**Outcome: inconclusive as a decryption claim.** Successful arithmetic is a real result. The supplied rules do not yet uniquely select and read the full matrix, and this experiment does not establish whether the proposed passage was intended.\n\n[Open the full-size coverage map](exports/figures/totient-map-coverage.svg) · [Open the node-choice diagram](exports/figures/totient-map-node-choice.svg)\n\n## How the map is made\n\nRead [LP2-00](#/page/lp2-00), [LP2-01](#/page/lp2-01) and [LP2-02](#/page/lp2-02) in that order. Keep every rune, including the heading, remove punctuation and spacing, and fill rows of 27 from left to right. Coordinates start at (1,1). This gives exactly 729 cells; the repository's displayed map agrees cell by cell. It is a rearrangement of the text, not the original page layout.\n\nThe coverage figure highlights only ciphertext cells used in the primary route. Keys and navigation landmarks can use other cells. There are 61 output positions but only 54 distinct ciphertext cells because several are read more than once. Reuse is not automatically an error in a geometric cipher; it needs an explicit rule, just as skipping cells does.\n\nFor the functions themselves, see [Euler’s totient](#/wiki/totient) and [the Möbius function](#/wiki/mobius-function).\n\n## A complete arithmetic example: WEATHER\n\nThe node at row 14, columns 4–6 is X–OE–X, with indices 14,22,14. Replace the middle index by its totient: φ(22)=10, giving X–I–X. Apply μ(φ(k)) to each derived key index. The signature is (1,0,1), whose sum modulo 3 is 2. Rotate the key left twice to get X–X–I and repeat it.\n\n| Cipher cell | Cipher index | Key index | Difference modulo 29 | Output |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| (14,14) | NG = 21 | X = 14 | 7 | W |\n| (14,15) | P = 13 | X = 14 | 28 | EA |\n| (14,16) | EO = 12 | I = 10 | 2 | TH |\n| (14,17) | O = 3 | X = 14 | 18 | E |\n| (14,18) | E = 18 | X = 14 | 4 | R |\n\nFive output runes spell WEATHER. This calculation does not itself explain why those five cells are chosen, why the block stops there, or which block follows. The opening block also crosses a row boundary, whereas later selections include vertical and diagonal segments. TURNS uses its three node indices directly rather than transforming the center. Those choices are preserved in the replay instead of silently replacing them with a uniform rule.\n\nThe output trace retains rune tokens such as TH and EA. Spaces and punctuation in the proposed English reading are editorial interpretations, not separate decoded symbols.\n\n## What the transition rules add\n\nThe source provides more than word examples. It predicts a next-key signature using Möbius values of current block coordinates. It switches between direct and half-turned positions at cumulative phase totals 7 and 14. A quarter-turn calculation updates the outer signature state. A separate formula involving the current beginning, end and original node center predicts horizontal, vertical or diagonal; another predicts whether the next block's leftmost cell is its beginning or end.\n\nWe recomputed all 16 primary transitions, treating OF and THE separately and using the primary SOON route. All three checks match. The starting state, block boundaries, node centers and phase thresholds are inputs. The source states that the thresholds were identified from this route. Consequently, **16 matches are an in-sample fit, not 16 held-out predictions**. The signature, axis and boundary checks also share inputs and must not be multiplied as independent probabilities.\n\n### How many keys share a signature?\n\nA signature constrains a key without identifying its runes. For example, (0,0,0) is shared by 4,096 ordered triples of positive rune indices; (1,0,1) by 1,296. These counts enumerate indices 1–28 only. They exclude F=0, for which the standard positive-integer totient is not defined here. They are not counts of reachable nodes: geometric restrictions can reduce the candidates considerably.\n\nFor each derived key index k, compute μ(φ(k)). Among indices 1–28, 16 give zero, 3 give −1, and 9 give +1. An ordered key with signature (0,0,0) can independently select any of the 16 zero-class indices in each slot: 16 × 16 × 16 = 4,096. Repeated indices are allowed in this algebraic count. The signature (1,0,1) similarly gives 9 × 16 × 9 = 1,296.\n\n[Inspect the signature-class diagram](exports/figures/totient-signature-classes.svg). These are derived key triples before phase rotation; equal outer signature values do not require equal outer rune indices. They do not enumerate manuscript locations, enforce mirror-node geometry, or measure how many alternatives survive the complete proposed traversal. Therefore they cannot be used as the denominator of a chance probability for the reading.\n\n### Check one transition by hand: WEATHER → TURNS\n\nWEATHER occupies absolute positions 365–369, where position is `27 × (row − 1) + column`. Its original key-node center is (14,5), position 356, and contains OE with rune index 22. The cumulative phase total before this transition is 2, so the direct-position mode with offset 1 applies.\n\n| Quantity | Calculation | Result |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Next phase | `(1 + μ(365) + μ(366) + μ(367) + μ(368) + μ(369)) mod 3` = `(1 + 1 − 1 − 1 + 0 + 0) mod 3` | 0 |\n| Next outer state | Quarter-turned positions are 365, 392, 419, 446, 473; minimum 365 has μ = 1. Update `(1 + 1) mod 2`. | 0 |\n| Next signature | Phase 0 and outer state 0 force the middle component to 0. | (0,0,0) |\n| Next axis | `μ(365 + 356) + μ(gcd(473,361))` = `μ(721) + μ(1)` = 1 + 1 | Positive: vertical |\n| Next boundary role | Three-quarter-turned endpoint has position 257. `(μ(257) + φ(22)) mod 2` = `(−1 + 10) mod 2` | 1: beginning |\n\nFor a vertical block, the minimum quarter-turned position corresponds to its bottommost cell. Calling that cell the beginning therefore predicts upward reading. The supplied TURNS block does read upward, from (14,19) to (10,19), and its key has signature (0,0,0). These properties agree; the calculation still does not choose column 19, the block's starting row, its length, or the exact key.\n\nEvery transition now has the same level of detail in the report's `calculation` object: coordinates, transformed positions, individual Möbius values, cumulative state, gcd arguments and boundary selection. The independent checker reconstructs these entries by rotating coordinates directly instead of using the replay's formulas for rotated absolute positions.\n\n## A controlled ambiguity: three SOON nodes\n\nThe source documents L–C–EA, L–I–EA and L–EO–EA. Their center indices 5, 10 and 12 all have totient 4. All therefore derive L–R–EA, align to EA–L–R, and turn the same X–D–W–H ciphertext into SOON.\n\nHowever, the next-axis formula also uses the original center's **position**. With the documented centers (25,7), (20,15) and (25,14), the scores are respectively 0, −1 and −1: horizontal, diagonal, diagonal. The published transition fit chooses (25,7), which agrees with THEN's horizontal block. The source explicitly identifies that choice.\n\nThis is a bounded example of a selection that affects the result. It does not prove that any desired sentence can be produced, or that all three choices satisfy every proposed navigation condition. It shows why a full decoder needs a rule selecting the original node before the next block is inspected.\n\n## Are three-rune mirrors unusual by themselves?\n\nWe counted equal outer runes around any center, along rows, columns and the two diagonals, at every in-bounds radius from 1 to 13. Each unoriented triple is counted once. The map has **507** such mirrors.\n\nAs a control, we shuffled the same 729 rune indices 99 times using seed 3301. This preserves rune frequencies but removes their original positions. Mirror counts ranged from **458 to 568**. The observed count is inside that range.\n\nThis control is deliberately narrow. It tests the abundance of this simple geometric pattern, not the quality of the proposed English, the complete traversal, or the combined transition rules. It supplies no chance probability for the selected reading. Testing that stronger claim would require a completely specified search procedure, the same search budget on controls, and a scoring rule chosen before inspecting the results.\n\n## How to reproduce\n\nDownload this experiment's bundle and extract it without changing its folder structure. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient; no network, API or model is required.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/totient-map-route/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/totient-map-route/check.py\npython experiments/records/totient-map-route/signature_figure.py\n```\n\nThe first command rebuilds the report and coverage image in memory and compares them with the saved versions. It checks all selected key nodes and subtractions, recomputes transition matches, enumerates signature classes, and repeats the mirror controls. Running without `--check` writes the report and coverage image. The explanatory node-choice diagram is an authored illustration of the reported three-node comparison.\n\nThe second command independently derives totients through prime factorization, checks all 65 recorded rune subtractions and node-derived keys, and compares totients with coprime counting for 1–729. It also independently verifies all 16 transition calculation records, all 18 key-node midpoints, and rotation identities for all 729 cells. It does not independently rediscover the route or certify the author's navigation choices. The JSON report includes all rune traces, transition inputs/results, the 99 control counts, reused cells, and phase-rotation ablations. Those ablations deliberately change the phase rule; they are sensitivity checks, not alternatives permitted by the fixed phase formula.\n\nThe third command independently calculates totients by counting coprimes and Möbius values by factorization, checks all six reported signature-class counts, and verifies the saved diagram. Add `--write` only to regenerate that diagram. It does not search for map nodes or produce plaintext.\n\n## What would strengthen the claim\n\nA useful next variant would freeze a deterministic procedure for choosing the initial node, subsequent anchors, node transformations, distance expressions, block lengths, directions, stopping condition and tie-breaking. It should specify how to handle zero-valued runes and every branch that remains possible.\n\nRun that fixed procedure on an unseen continuation before adjusting it. Report all outputs, not only readable ones. If alternatives remain, bound the enumeration and apply an explicit score to every candidate and to matched controls. This is the distinction between a reproducible selected reading and a decoder capable of making a new prediction. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [planning a first experiment](#/wiki/first-experiment).\n\nThe numerical and thematic correspondences in the source's “Strongest Plaintext Evidence” discussion are not assigned significance here. Nor does this test rule out other 27 × 27, totient or geometric methods. Revisions that change node selection or traversal belong as related variants in this experiment family, with their changed choices stated explicitly.\n",

    {
      "path": "experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/correction-effects.svg",
      "caption": "Eight stored corrections compared by mark edits, ordered runes, and normalized rune tokens. This summarizes the tested data layers; it is not a new image reading."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Do the stored transcription corrections change the published LP2 word-length statistics?\n\nFor the **seven currently stored LP2 reviewed-text layers**, no. Applying them all leaves the ordered rune stream, rune-token sequence, 2,896-token length distribution, and whole-stream IoC pair counts unchanged under the site's published counting rule. The one LP1 reviewed layer is a useful positive control: LP1-10 swaps two neighboring runes, changing six ordered-bigram type counts, while retaining its rune multiset and token-length sequence.\n\nThis is a sensitivity measurement of the stored layers, **not** a fresh verification of the manuscript images. It says nothing about corrections not yet recorded. A method that treats every punctuation mark as a key reset can change even when this particular word-length statistic does not.\n\n![Per-page correction effects: mark edits, rune order, and rune-token sequence](experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/correction-effects.svg)\n\n## Inputs and rules\n\nUse the archived `raw` and separate `reviewed_text` in the eight page records: LP1-10; LP2-05, 07, 11, 15, 35, 37 and 38. These are the only eight records with a distinct reviewed layer in the current [75-page inventory](#/wiki/transcription-checking?section=coverage). Every input page record and the 29-rune alphabet are pinned by SHA-256 in `plan.json`.\n\nFor word lengths, concatenate LP2-00 through LP2-55 in order, remove slash and CR/LF row wraps, keep headings, and identify runs of the 29 runes with optional internal apostrophes. Other punctuation separates tokens. Count runes, not Latin transliteration letters. This is the same rule used by the [word-length census](#/wiki/word-lengths). No alternative punctuation policy or page-local tokenization is included in the main comparison.\n\nThe seven LP2 corrections consist of added or removed notation marks, with no rune substitution. The LP1-10 correction swaps the runes at zero-based rune indices 116 and 117; it is outside the LP2 corpus. The independent checker reconstructs all seven LP2 reviewed strings from the documented edit offsets and checks the LP1 adjacent swap separately.\n\n## Measured effect\n\n| Page | Stored change | Ordered runes | Rune-token sequence | Token count |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |\n| LP1-10 | Adjacent rune swap | Changed | Changed | 40 → 40 |\n| LP2-05 | Add `-` | Same | Same | 59 → 59 |\n| LP2-07 | Add `.` | Same | Same | 50 → 50 |\n| LP2-11 | Add `-` | Same | Same | 55 → 55 |\n| LP2-15 | Add `.` | Same | Same | 37 → 37 |\n| LP2-35 | Add an apostrophe | Same | Same after omitting the apostrophe | 61 → 61 |\n| LP2-37 | Remove three `-` and one `.` | Same | Same | 53 → 53 |\n| LP2-38 | Add `.` | Same | Same | 47 → 47 |\n\nAcross LP2-00–55, both versions contain **12,956 runes**, **2,896 rune tokens**, and a maximum token length of **14**. Their complete token-length histograms match. Their whole-stream IoC numerator and denominator are **5,787,026 / 167,844,980** in both versions. The ordered rune stream and normalized token sequence have matching SHA-256 values. LP2-35's literal token text contains an extra apostrophe; the apostrophe is not a rune, and its normalized rune token is unchanged.\n\nLP1-10 demonstrates that the audit can register a real ordered-rune difference: the two-rune exchange changes six ordered-bigram type counts. Because it is a swap, its rune count, multiset and whole-page IoC remain unchanged. Its word lengths remain 40 tokens with the same length sequence, even though the token containing the swapped symbols has different rune order.\n\n## What follows—and what does not\n\nFor these exact stored LP2 corrections, recomputing the site's joined-page word-length histogram will not change the result. A rune-only frequency or IoC calculation also receives the same symbols in the same order. This is stronger than merely saying that punctuation changes *might* affect word lengths: it measures the actual published corrections under a declared tokenizer.\n\nIt does **not** prove that punctuation is irrelevant. A period, hyphen or apostrophe can drive a reset or extraction rule that this experiment does not run. Different tokenization, image-derived separators, or a newly corrected rune can change later measurements. Nor does matching a reviewed layer establish that the image was transcribed correctly everywhere. See [the transcription guide](#/wiki/transcription-checking) for the distinction between archived text, reviewed correction and original-image evidence.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root or extracted experiment ZIP, with Python 3 and no packages:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command recomputes every page and the complete LP2 corpus, then compares `results.json` and the SVG. The second independently reconstructs the reviewed strings and scans rune tokens with a separate parser. `run.py` without flags prints a compact summary. The full machine-readable result includes per-page histograms, correction fields, hashes and the exact IoC pair counts.\n\nThe next variants should test a *specified* punctuation-sensitive key clock or tokenization policy, then add newly image-reviewed disputed marks one at a time. Retain this archived-versus-reviewed baseline so any changed conclusion can be attributed to the exact edit that caused it.\n\nFor a more specific statistic on the same seven LP2 reviewed layers, the [doublet boundary audit](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries) checks all 86 equal-rune pairs and whether any stored mark edit changes the intervening-separator class.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/article.md",

      "path": "experiments/records/uniform-additive-doublets/distribution.svg",
      "caption": "Binomial probabilities in ten-count bins under independent uniform additive keys. The observed count is 86; the expected count is about 445. Display ends at 649, with the remaining probability retained in JSON. This is a specific model comparison, not a plaintext-language probability."
